Measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation

Francesco Albarelli Email: francesco.albarelli@gmail.com Affiliation: Università di Parma, Dipartimento di Scienze Matematiche, Fisiche e Informatiche, I-43124 Parma, Italy Affiliation: INFN—Sezione di Milano-Bicocca, gruppo collegato di Parma, I-43124 Parma, Italy    Dominic Branford Email: dominic.branford@unifi.it Affiliation: Dipartimento di Fisica e Astronomia, Università di Firenze, via G. Sansone 1, I-50019 Sesto Fiorentino (FI), Italy    Jesús Rubio Email: jesus@rubiojimenez.com Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Physics, University of Surrey, Guildford GU2 7XH, United Kingdom Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Exeter, Stocker Road, Exeter EX4 4QL, United Kingdom
3rd August 2026
Abstract

We present a comprehensive and pedagogical formulation of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. Within this framework, we analyse the role of measurement incompatibility and establish its quantitative effect on attainable precision. We achieve this by deriving upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement—a notion from hypothesis testing—combined with the evaluation of the Nagaoka–Hayashi lower bound. In general, we prove that, as in the many-copy regime of local estimation theory, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario in which individually optimal measurements are assumed jointly implementable. Therefore, in practical situations, the latter may provide a sufficient and computationally efficient benchmark without solving the full optimisation problem. Our results, which we illustrate through applications of discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, including an open-source package for all the bounds discussed here.

1 Introduction

Quantum metrology explores the fundamental and practical impact of quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition, squeezing, and entanglement, on high-precision measurements of physical parameters [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Its central aim is to surpass the precision limits of classical strategies that do not rely on these quantum effects. Even if such advantage is not always feasible, a proper understanding of the fundamental precision limits imposed by quantum mechanics is crucial to develop new technologies and guide resource allocation [6, 7, 8].

Quantum estimation theory (QET) provides the mathematical framework for analysing the precision limits achievable with quantum systems. Its most celebrated result is the quantum Cramér–Rao bound (CRB) [9]. While many results in quantum metrology rely on the CRB, this approach has important limitations. Roughly speaking, the CRB is a meaningful figure of merit only when a large number of experiment repetitions is performed, with a significant caveat that it is often hard to understand a priori how many repetitions are needed. This flavour of QET is known as local, meaning that its predictions are generally valid when the discrepancy between the estimates and the true value of the parameters is sufficiently small, which eventually happens as samples accumulate.

Global estimation theory [10, 11] represents a complementary approach that is especially relevant when resources are constrained and only a limited number of experimental trials can be performed [12, 13, 14]. While several global approaches have been proposed [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23], the most established and extensively developed framework for going beyond the local estimation paradigm is Bayesian quantum estimation. Dating back to the early days of the field [24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 9], it is nowadays being increasingly applied to a wide range of multiparameter sensing experiments involving both photons [30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35], atoms [36, 37], and solid-state systems [38]. This is the framework adopted in the present work.

Bayesian estimation is not only practically significant in regimes with limited experimental data but also holds deep fundamental implications. For example, it clarifies impractical claims arising from applying local QET beyond its valid domain, such as the alleged effectiveness of super-Heisenberg-limited schemes [39, 12, 40] or the apparent enhancement in multiple phase estimation [41, 42, 43, 44], and it reveals the need to correct the Heisenberg limit in phase estimation by a factor of π\pi [45]. In general, the strategies predicted by local QET can become suboptimal in the non-asymptotic regime [20], where the Bayesian framework consistently enables efficient information extraction [13, 46]. This is unsurprising given that Bayesian inference constitutes the most basic form of learning [47], which is the most comprehensive approach for characterising quantum systems [48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56].

One of the fundamental aspects of quantum theory is the existence of incompatible measurements that cannot be implemented jointly [57, 58]. In the context of quantum metrology, this phenomenon becomes crucial when multiple parameters must be estimated simultaneously: measurement incompatibility can impose fundamental trade-offs on the achievable precision of different parameters [59, 60, 61, 62], which have been quantified in various ways [63, 64, 65, 66]. Besides this concrete consequence, incompatibility makes multiparameter theory mathematically challenging [10]. While the fundamental precision limits in single-parameter quantum metrology are relatively well-understood, fundamental multiparameter limits remain a subject of active research [67, 68, 69].

It is instructive to review the impact of such incompatibility effects on the development of local QET, before drawing a parallel with the Bayesian approach. A multiparameter version of the quantum CRB was first derived by Helstrom at the dawn of the field, based on the notion of the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) [70, 9]. We shall call this bound the Helstrom (SLD) CRB. While this bound proved attainable for single-parameter estimation [71, 72], it does not account for the effects of incompatibility and is not generally attainable for multiparameter estimation. In the following decades, further quantum generalisations of the CRB were developed, providing a better account of measurement incompatibility, and culminating in the discovery that the ultimate precision limit attainable with collective (entangling) measurements over many copies is given by the Holevo–Cramér–Rao bound (HCRB) [10, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77]. It was eventually understood that, in this asymptotic scenario where many copies can be measured collectively, the effect of measurement incompatibility is relatively mild: the HCRB can be at most twice the original bound obtained by Helstrom [78, 79] (see also Refs. [67, 10, 64]).

By contrast, the fundamental precision achievable with separable measurements on each copy of the state is not efficiently computable in local QET, even numerically (although collective measurements are unnecessary for pure states [80]). Nonetheless, several bounds for this setting have been derived [81, 82, 83, 84, 85, 86], among which we highlight the Nagaoka–Hayashi (NH) bound [87, 88, 89, 90, 91, 92, 93, 94]. Most recently, the problem has been studied using conic programming [95], providing a unifying framework and new tools that have already been applied to probe state optimisation [96].

Despite significant advances in local QET, the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian estimation has received much less attention. The general conditions that a Bayesian estimation strategy must satisfy to be optimal were already identified in the aforementioned early works [26, 27, 29, 9], including a discrete analogue for hypothesis testing [97, 98]. A generalisation to convex functions has also been proposed [99]. Ref. [9] provided examples of how these conditions can be used to verify whether a proposed strategy is indeed optimal. Reversing this procedure—namely, using the conditions to derive the optimal strategy—is, however, exceedingly challenging, with only a limited number of problems where this can be done analytically. For instance, this procedure can be carried out in the simple case of two parameters [100].

For single-parameter estimation, the class of location-isomorphic estimation problems can be optimised exactly [101], and the solution can be shown to satisfy the corresponding optimality conditions. This family includes, as a particular case, the optimisation of the standard mean square error—called mean square loss (MSL) in this work—a problem originally solved by Personick [25]. While Personick made an early attempt to extend this reasoning to the estimation of two parameters [24], closed-form solutions based on indirect measurements were subsequently obtained [102], and a solution for the estimation of two displacement parameters in Gaussian states with Gaussian priors is known [103], a general and practical procedure for determining optimal solutions in the Bayesian estimation of multiple parameters has remained elusive for decades.

Only recently has a multiparameter bound, analogous to the Helstrom (SLD) CRB—and thus neglecting incompatibility effects—been derived [43]. As motivated later, we propose referring to this as the symmetric posterior mean (SPM) bound. Bayesian analogues of several other local bounds, including the NH bound, have since been established, incorporating measurement incompatibility to a certain extent [104, 105]. In addition, numerical algorithms for identifying optimal estimation strategies are now under active investigation [106, 107].

Continuing the parallel between the local and Bayesian frameworks, this work addresses a key question: how strongly does measurement incompatibility affect Bayesian multiparameter QET? In other words, what is the maximal discrepancy between the achievable precision and the bound that neglect incompatibility?

Contributions.—We show that, in analogy with local QET, the minimum MSL can be at most twice the SPM benchmark that is obtained when measurement incompatibility is ignored. Key differences, however, are that this upper bound now holds at the single-shot level, but can also be trivial, i.e., larger than the MSL derived solely from a priori information. This effect stems from the central role of prior information in Bayesian estimation, which, as illustrated through examples in quantum imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, may significantly modify the apparent incompatibility of the estimation protocol. Consequently, measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter QET is not only a relatively mild factor in the overall estimation precision, but it can also be concealed when the influence of the prior is strong. We further derive a tighter upper bound that is guaranteed to be non-trivial, by combining measurements introduced in hypothesis testing [108, 109, 110, 111] with optimal classical Bayes estimators [47]. Our upper bounds are complementary to existing lower bounds tighter than the SPM one, where the Bayesian NH bound [104] represents the state of the art. In addition, we derive a class of lower bounds based on generalised posterior mean operators beyond the symmetric version that, while less tight than the NH bound, may be of independent interest, since they are obtained via the theory of monotone metrics, analogously to established results in local QET [112]. An open-source code for the numerical evaluation of all relevant bounds is available on GitHub [113]. Finally, beyond deriving bounds on the minimum MSL, we determine explicit conditions for the measurement strategies that achieve it. Combined with the pedagogical and self-contained introduction to Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology presented in this work, these results establish a solid foundation for further advances in the field.

2 Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation theory

2.1 Preliminaries

Let 𝚯\boldsymbol{\Theta} denote a vector of unknown parameters and 𝜽∈Ω\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\Omega a vector hypotheses—values the unknown parameter could take—both understood as d×1d{\times}1 column vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Here, Ω\Omega represents a generic parameter space. The information about 𝚯\boldsymbol{\Theta} available prior to any measurement is encoded in a probability density p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}), satisfying the non-negativity and normalisation conditions:

p⁡(𝜽)≥0,∫Ωd​𝜽​p​(𝜽)=1.p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\geq 0,\quad\int_{\Omega}\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})=1. (1)

This p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is referred to as the prior probability.

To gather information about 𝚯\boldsymbol{\Theta} via measurements, the vector hypothesis is encoded in the quantum state of a suitable physical system, such as an atomic ensemble or a Mach–Zehnder interferometer, denoted by ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}). This is a positive semidefinite operator with unit trace:

ρ⁡(𝜽)⪰0,Tr⁡[ρ⁡(𝜽)]=1.\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\succeq 0,\quad\operatorname{Tr}[\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})]=1. (2)

We focus on finite-dimensional quantum systems, and whilst we expect most results in Sec. 3 to hold more generally, we leave a more rigorous analysis for future work.

Once a state ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is prepared, a measurement with outcome x∈χx\in\chi is performed, where χ\chi denotes the sampling space. Each outcome is associated with an element M⁡(x)M(x) of a positive operator-valued measure (POVM), which is positive semidefinite and resolves the identity:

M⁡(x)⪰0,∫χd​x​M​(x)=𝕀.M(x)\succeq 0,\quad\int_{\chi}\mathrm{d}x\,M(x)=\mathbb{I}. (3)

For simplicity, in Sec. 4, we only consider examples with discrete outcomes, which is natural when focusing on finite-dimensional systems. In such cases, continuous outcomes can be realised by performing finite measurements depending on a classical parameter [114]. Conversely, discrete outcomes can be embedded in a continuous-outcome formulation by expressing M⁡(x)M(x) as a sum of Dirac delta functions centered on the discrete outcome nn,

M⁡(x)=∑nMn​δ​(x−n),M(x)=\sum_{n}M_{n}\,\delta(x-n), (4)

associated with a POVM element MnM_{n} satisfying Mn⪰0M_{n}\succeq 0 and ∑nMn=𝕀\sum_{n}M_{n}=\mathbb{I}. The continuous-outcome formalism is particularly convenient for variational calculus, which is frequently employed in Bayesian optimisation [25, 47].

At this point, Bayesian inference offers a straightforward solution to the problem of inferring the value of 𝚯\boldsymbol{\Theta} by combining Bayes’ theorem with the Born rule. Specifically, the prior probability p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is updated according to

p⁡(𝜽)↦p⁡(𝜽|x)∝p⁡(𝜽)​Tr​[M⁡(x)​ρ​(𝜽)].p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\mapsto p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|x)\propto p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\Tr[M(x)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})]. (5)

Here, the probability density p⁡(𝜽|x)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|x) denotes the posterior probability while Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ​(𝜽)]=p⁡(x|𝜽)\Tr[M(x)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})]=p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta}) is identified as the likelihood function.

The posterior probability represents the full state of knowledge about the values of the parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} available after observing the measurement outcome xx. In that sense, it could be already considered a complete solution of the problem.

Calculation of the posterior probabilities underpins all Bayesian measurement protocols. However, more ergonomical theoretical constructions are generally required. For instance, it is customary to identify a single vector value representing our best guess for the unknown 𝚯\boldsymbol{\Theta}. Intuitively, one possibility is taking the vector of parameters that maximises the posterior probability, which is particularly suitable in situations with a unimodal Gaussian profile. That is,

𝜽~MAP​(x)=arg⁡max𝜽⁡p⁡(𝜽|x).\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}_{\mathrm{MAP}}(x)=\arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|x). (6)

This is the so-called maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator [115], which plays a role similar to that of the maximum likelihood estimator in local QET [116].

Furthermore, to select a state ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and a POVM element M⁡(x)M(x) and guide optimal experimental design, together with an estimator 𝜽~​(x)\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}(x) for post-processing the data, one requires a figure of merit that quantifies estimation performance and serves as the optimisation criterion. To that end, one typically introduces a loss function11 1 This function is also often referred to as a cost, deviation, or error function. The term loss is preferred because it conveys a general notion of estimation inaccuracy, encompassing statistical, systematic, and context-dependent sources. In contrast, deviation and error typically emphasise purely statistical discrepancies, whereas cost may suggest application-specific considerations more typical of engineering contexts. l⁡(𝜽,𝜽~)l(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}) quantifying the inaccuracy that may arise by choosing an estimate 𝜽~\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}} should the hypothesis 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} correspond to the true parameter values [47]. An estimator, state, and POVM are then said to be optimal when they minimise the mean loss

ℒ≔∫d​𝜽​𝑑x​p​(𝜽)​Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ​(𝜽)]​l​(𝜽~​(x),𝜽),\mathcal{L}\coloneq\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\Tr[M(x)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})]\,l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}(x),\boldsymbol{\theta}), (7)

where, for simplicity, we omit explicit reference to the domains Ω\Omega and χ\chi. This convention will be followed henceforth.

This work evaluates measurement incompatibility within the Bayesian paradigm by establishing lower and upper bounds on a particular type of mean loss ℒ\mathcal{L}. The remainder of this section addresses formal aspects of ℒ\mathcal{L}, as well as the notion of metrological optimality based on this figure of merit, that are necessary to derive and contextualise our main results in Sec. 3.

2.2 Estimation performance

We first observe that Eq. (7) quantifies estimation performance by integrating over all hypothesis values in Ω\Omega, whose contribution can vary from small to large, weighted by the prior probability p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}). This is the key feature that makes the framework not only global but also Bayesian. There exists a more conservative, non-Bayesian approach to global estimation: the minimax approach, which is based on the frequentist loss [6]

ℒ⁡(𝜽)≔∫d​x​Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ​(𝜽)]​l​(𝜽~​(x),𝜽),\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\coloneq\int\mathrm{d}x\,\Tr[M(x)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})]\,l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}(x),\boldsymbol{\theta}), (8)

and seeks to minimise the worst-case value of ℒ⁡(𝜽)\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) over relevant regions of the parameter space [117]. However, since the minimax criterion can be written as the supremum of Eq. (7) over all priors, our bounds in Sec. 3 are also relevant for minimax estimation. Note that, at the other extreme, Eq. (8) is employed in local QET by evaluating it in an infinitesimal neighbourhood of specific values of 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} [116, 6].

We further comment that, in Bayesian estimation, the additional integral over xx is required only when searching for optimal estimation protocols, as in our case, since this task precedes the recording of specific outcomes. For data post-processing, estimation performance must instead be assessed using an outcome-dependent quantifier [118], e.g.,

ℒ⁡(x)≔∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽|x)​l​(𝜽~​(x),𝜽).\mathcal{L}(x)\coloneq\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|x)\,l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}(x),\boldsymbol{\theta}). (9)

Alternatively, one may employ credibility intervals, also based on the posterior [118, 119]. Both experimental error assessment and the minimax and local estimation approaches discussed above are beyond the scope of this work, and we therefore focus exclusively on Eq. (7).

So far we have not specified any loss function ll. The most prevalent choice is

l⁡(𝜽~,𝜽)=(𝜽~−𝜽)T​L​(𝜽~−𝜽),l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})=(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta})^{T}L\,(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}), (10)

where LL is a positive semidefinite weight matrix, i.e., L⪰0L\succeq 0, and we assume it to be parameter-independent. The resulting ℒ\mathcal{L} is the standard MSL, and this loss quantifier leads to the posterior mean (PM) as the optimal Bayes estimator [47]:

θ~opt,i​(x)=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽|x)​θi=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽)​θi∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽).\tilde{\theta}_{\mathrm{opt},i}(x)=\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|x)\,\theta_{i}=\frac{\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{i}}{\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})}. (11)

There is a widespread belief that the MSL applies universally, regardless of the specific system, measurement, or type of parameters of interest. Strictly speaking, however, the MSL is only appropriate for location or shift parameters. This is because the topology for such parameters corresponds to the real line, so that the corresponding loss function must be translation invariant [47], i.e.,

l⁡(𝜽~+𝜸,𝜽+𝜸)=l⁡(𝜽~,𝜽),l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}+\boldsymbol{\gamma},\boldsymbol{\theta}+\boldsymbol{\gamma})=l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta}), (12)

as Eq. (10) is22 2 While one can generally consider parameter-dependent weight matrices, these break the translation invariance of Eq. (10).. Here, 𝜸\boldsymbol{\gamma} is an arbitrary constant vector.

In contrast, parameter types with different properties require alternative loss functions. Cycle parameters, for instance, are estimated using trigonometric loss functions—phases in interferometry are the archetypical example [9, 120, 6]. Moreover, recent results show that scale parameters such as temperature or decay rate require logarithmic loss functions for consistent estimation [121], while weight parameters such as probability of success or coherence parameters demand hyperbolic loss functions [122]. Naive use of the MSL, while it may occasionally yield correct results—particularly when 𝚯\boldsymbol{\Theta} is known to lie close to a reference point 𝚯0\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{0}—is physically unjustified and therefore discouraged unless there is no better choice.

Despite this, one can retain the mathematical simplicity of the MSL while respecting parameters’ more general topologies in certain scenarios. Specifically, Refs. [101, 123] demonstrated that many parameter types admit mean losses equivalent to the MSL, up to a mapping that, in the context of multiparameter estimation, can be expressed as

l⁡(𝜽~,𝜽)=(𝒇⁡(𝜽~)−𝒇⁡(𝜽))T​L​(𝒇⁡(𝜽~)−𝒇⁡(𝜽)),l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})=(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\theta}))^{T}L\,(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\theta})), (13)

where 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} is chosen according to symmetries of the problem [122]; see Ref. [37] for an experimental demonstration with cold Cs\mathrm{Cs} atoms. Note that phases fall outside this framework [120], though they can be approximated by the MSL itself when confined to intervals of order π/2\pi/2 [8, 13].

Our results in Sec. 3 are formulated in terms of the standard MSL for pedagogical reasons, but the extension to Eq. (13) is immediate. While a general multiparameter symmetry-informed treatment is deferred, Sec. 4.2 provides an illustration of how to use Eq. (13).

2.3 Optimal quantum strategies

We proceed by providing the conditions that minimise the MSL and tools to establish an operational notion of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. For a fixed measurement, the optimal classical estimator is the posterior mean (PM), already introduced in Eq. (11). In the quantum setting, however, one must also minimise the MSL over all generalised measurements, thereby making the optimisation substantially more challenging.

To ease the manipulation of multiparameter expressions, we first rewrite the MSL as

ℒ=λ+Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ0​Mj​i−2​ρ¯j​Mi].\mathcal{L}=\lambda+L^{ij}\,\Tr[\rho_{0}M_{ji}-2\bar{\rho}_{j}M_{i}]. (14)

Here, λ\lambda is the weighted second moment of the prior probability,

λ≔∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝜽T​L​𝜽,\lambda\coloneq\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}L\,\boldsymbol{\theta}, (15)

which differs from the a priori MSL for nonvanishing prior mean, i.e., when ∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​θi≠0\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{i}\neq 0 for at least some ii; see Eq. (37) and App. A. The element Li​jL^{ij} denotes the i​jij-th component of LL, and we employ the Einstein summation convention over indices i,j=1,…,di,j=1,\dots,d.

We further define, respectively, the following zeroth and first state moments:

ρ0\displaystyle\rho_{0} :=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ρ​(𝜽),\displaystyle:=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}), (16a)
ρ¯i\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{i} :=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ρ​(𝜽)​θi,\displaystyle:=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{i}, (16b)

as well as the following first and second measurement moments:

Mi\displaystyle M_{i} :=∫d​x​M​(x)​θ~i​(x)=∫d​𝜽~​M​(𝜽~)​θ~i,\displaystyle:=\int\mathrm{d}x\,M(x)\,\tilde{\theta}_{i}(x)=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}\,M(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\,\tilde{\theta}_{i}, (17a)
Mi​j\displaystyle M_{ij} :=∫d​x​M​(x)​θ~i​(x)​θ~j​(x)=∫d​𝜽~​M​(𝜽~)​θ~i​θ~j,\displaystyle:=\int\mathrm{d}x\,M(x)\,\tilde{\theta}_{i}(x)\tilde{\theta}_{j}(x)=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}\,M(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\,\tilde{\theta}_{i}\tilde{\theta}_{j}, (17b)

where to obtain the rightmost expressions we have combined the estimators and the measurement by using the relabelled POVM elements [10]

M⁡(𝜽~)=∫d​x​M​(x)​δ​(𝜽~−𝜽~​(x));M(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})=\int\mathrm{d}x\,M(x)\,\delta(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}(x)); (18)

this will be useful in following calculations.

Given that p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) must be fixed a priori, and LL is fixed according to the priority assigned to certain linear combinations or specific parameters, λ\lambda remains constant throughout. The degrees of freedom for optimising the MSL are thus ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and either the pair (𝜽~​(x),M​(x))(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}(x),M(x)) or, as we will consider from now on, M⁡(𝜽~)M(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}). Since our focus is measurement incompatibility, and not the trade-offs that arise from the choice of probing strategy before the final measurement [124, 125, 126], we shall also assume that ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})—and therefore ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ¯i\bar{\rho}_{i}—is fixed.

The general conditions constraining the form of the optimal M⁡(𝜽~)M(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}), denoted Mopt​(𝜽~)M_{\mathrm{opt}}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}), have been established since the seminal works of Personick, Helstrom, Holevo, and others [25, 26, 27, 28, 9, 127] in the 1970s. In App. B, we revisit these conditions and show that, for the MSL, they read

Li​j[\displaystyle L^{ij}[ (θ~j​θ~i​𝕀−Mopt,j​i)​ρ0+ρ0​(θ~j​θ~i​𝕀−Mopt,j​i)\displaystyle(\tilde{\theta}_{j}\tilde{\theta}_{i}\mathbb{I}-M_{\mathrm{opt},ji})\rho_{0}+\rho_{0}(\tilde{\theta}_{j}\tilde{\theta}_{i}\mathbb{I}-M_{\mathrm{opt},ji}) (19)
−2(θ~j𝕀−Mopt,j)ρ¯i−2ρ¯j(θ~i𝕀−Mopt,i)]⪰0,\displaystyle-2(\tilde{\theta}_{j}\mathbb{I}-M_{\mathrm{opt},j})\bar{\rho}_{i}-2\bar{\rho}_{j}(\tilde{\theta}_{i}\mathbb{I}-M_{\mathrm{opt},i})]\succeq 0,

for all 𝜽~\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}. Here, Mopt,i​jM_{\mathrm{opt},ij} and Mopt,iM_{\mathrm{opt},i} are obtained by inserting Mopt​(𝜽~)M_{\mathrm{opt}}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}) into Eqs. (17). This leads to the minimum mean loss

ℒmin=ℒ⁡[Mopt​(𝜽~)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}=\mathcal{L}[M_{\mathrm{opt}}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})], (20)

i.e., ℒ\mathcal{L} in Eq. (14) evaluated at the optimal POVM.

Eq. (19) constitutes our first result. In general, determining the explicit form of Mopt​(𝜽~)M_{\mathrm{opt}}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}) from Eq. (19) is a nontrivial task. Nevertheless, these conditions provide a practical criterion for verifying whether a candidate POVM is truly optimal. Note that employing a symmetry-informed yet still quadratic loss function [Eq. (13)] yields optimality conditions of the same structure, with the parameter space remapped according to the vector symmetry function 𝒇\boldsymbol{f}.

2.4 Lower bounds from optimal single-parameter strategies

While exact computation of ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}} is generally difficult, it admits a lower bound [43, 128, 10]

ℒmin≥λ−Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ0​Sj​Si]≕ℒSPM,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}\geq\lambda-L^{ij}\Tr[\rho_{0}S_{j}S_{i}]\eqqcolon\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}, (21)

where {Si}\{S_{i}\} are the SPM operators, defined as the solutions to the Lyapunov equations

ρ¯i=Si​ρ0+ρ0​Si2=Eρ0,S​[Si].\bar{\rho}_{i}=\frac{S_{i}\rho_{0}+\rho_{0}S_{i}}{2}=E_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{S}}\left[S_{i}\right]. (22)

For later convenience, we have introduced the anticommutator map (superoperator)

Eρ,S​[X]≔12​(X​ρ+ρ​X),E_{\rho,\mathrm{S}}[X]\coloneq\frac{1}{2}\left(X\rho+\rho X\right), (23)

which admits a compact expression Si=Eρ0,S−1​[ρ¯i]{S_{i}=E_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{S}}^{-1}[\bar{\rho}_{i}]} for the SPMs, and thus

ℒSPM=λ−Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ¯j​Eρ0,S−1​[ρ¯i]].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}=\lambda-L^{ij}\Tr[\bar{\rho}_{j}E_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{S}}^{-1}[\bar{\rho}_{i}]]. (24)

Here and in the rest of this work, we assume that this inverse exists, which is guaranteed for a full-rank ρ0\rho_{0}. When this is not the case, one simply needs to work in the relevant subspace spanned by the parametric family ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}), which corresponds to the support of ρ0\rho_{0}33 3 This is possible because the support of the operators {ρ¯j}\{\bar{\rho}_{j}\} is contained in the support of ρ0\rho_{0}, since ⟨ψ|ρ0|ψ⟩=0\braket{\psi|\rho_{0}|\psi}=0 implies ⟨ψ|ρ⁡(𝜽)|ψ⟩=0\braket{\psi|\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})|\psi}=0 almost everywhere (in the measure-theoretic sense), which in turn implies ⟨ψ|ρ¯j|ψ⟩=0\braket{\psi|\bar{\rho}_{j}|\psi}=0. This is markedly different from local QET, where the partial derivatives operators may have components also in the kernel of the state, and properties of rank-deficient models are non-trivial. For example, necessary and sufficient conditions for attainability of the SLD CRB are not fully characterised [129, 130, 91, 131] (except for pure states [80, 132]).

We note that several names have been adopted in the recent literature for the operators {Si}\{S_{i}\}, mostly in analogy with the SLD operators that appear in local QET. We propose instead the term SPM operators, by analogy with the optimal classical Bayes estimator for each parameter in Eq. (11).

Formally, the PM estimator is the component-wise ratio of the first-moment probability vector ∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽)​θi\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{i} to the average probability vector ∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽)\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta}). Intuitively, if p⁡(x|𝜽)p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta}) is formally replaced by a density operator ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}), there are infinitely many inequivalent ways to “divide” ρ¯i\bar{\rho}_{i} by ρ0\rho_{0}. The SPMs correspond to the symmetric choice, where “multiplication by ρ0\rho_{0}” is implemented by the map Eρ0,SE_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{S}}. Infinitely many other choices are possible and become inequivalent whenever ρ¯i\bar{\rho}_{i} and ρ0\rho_{0} do not commute, leading to different lower bounds; see App. D. This intuitive reasoning was originally identified by Personick [25] and is semantically consistent with local QET, in which the logarithmic derivative of a probability distribution admits inequivalent operator generalisations in the quantum setting [112].

Crucially, the SPM bound has the additional property of being attainable in single-parameter estimation by projecting onto the eigenbasis of the single SPM operator available in that case [25, 43, 10, 133]. Consequently, upon performing the eigendecomposition

Si=∑n|si,n⟩​⟨si,n|​si,nS_{i}=\sum_{n}\ket{s_{i,n}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{s_{i,n}}}s_{i,n} (25)

for the ii-th operator, where we assume a discrete eigenbasis for simplicity but without loss of generality, the spectrum {si,n}\{s_{i,n}\} defines the estimator (see Refs. [25, 133] for details, including a continuous-variable formulation)

si,n=∫d​θ​p​(θ|si,n)​θ=θ~opt,i​(n),s_{i,n}=\int\mathrm{d}\theta\,p(\theta|s_{i,n})\,\theta=\tilde{\theta}_{\mathrm{opt},i}(n), (26)

which naturally corresponds to the posterior mean (PM) estimator for the ii-th parameter.

While the PM estimators remain optimal in the multiparameter case [43], the SPM bound is generally not attainable due to the non-commutativity of the SPM operators. Nevertheless, it provides a valid lower bound on the minimum MSL and can be interpreted as the optimum obtained when incompatibility among the individually optimal measurements is neglected. Accordingly, the next section introduces a notion of measurement incompatibility based on ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}, establishing it as a result of Bayesian estimation theory analogous in fundamental significance to the Helstrom (SLD) CRB in local QET [10].

3 Measurement incompatibility: definition and bounds

3.1 Incompatibility figure of merit

As we have just argued, the benchmark to evaluate the impact of measurement incompatibility is the lower bound on the MSL, ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}, which is achievable when all SPM operators share a common eigenbasis and thence are compatible observables. Therefore, measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter estimation can be quantified by comparing ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}} with the minimum MSL achievable by measurements, ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}.

We introduce a figure of merit for measurement incompatibility of a given Bayesian multiparameter estimation problem as follows:

ℐ≔ℒminℒSPM−1≥0,\mathcal{I}\coloneq\frac{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}}{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}}-1\geq 0\,, (27)

where the inequality follows from the SPM lower bound in Eq. (21). A similar figure of merit has been studied also in the framework of local QET [64]. In the following sections, we shall derive upper and lower bounds on ℐ\mathcal{I} by obtaining corresponding bounds on the unknown ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}.

3.2 Upper bounds

The incompatibility quantifier ℐ\mathcal{I} can be upper bounded by considering specific POVMs and estimators, since the corresponding MSL is, by definition, never smaller than the achievable minimum.

3.2.1 Pretty good measurement

Taking inspiration from hypothesis testing, we introduce the square root measurement, also known as the pretty good measurement (PGM) [108, 109, 110, 111]:

MPGM​(𝜽~)≔p⁡(𝜽~)​ρ0−12​ρ​(𝜽~)​ρ0−12.M_{\mathrm{PGM}}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\coloneq p(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\rho(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}. (28)

This measurement is usually introduced for discriminating among discrete hypotheses, where the Barnum–Knill theorem guarantees the “pretty good” performance [134]. Recently, this theorem has been extended to continuous hypotheses [135] and applied to prove that the MSL of the PGM is within a factor two of the optimal ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}. While this remarkable result establishes the usefulness of the PGM for parameter estimation, it does not shed light on the issue of measurement incompatibility, i.e., understanding the discrepancy between ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}} and ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}. This will be the precise topic of the next subsection. In the remainder of this subsection, we set the stage by deriving the expression for the MSL achieved by the PGM.

Before proceeding, it is important to emphasise that the PGM is a POVM with outcomes in the parameter space and therefore already incorporates a classical estimator, which may not be optimal. Nonetheless, it yields simple expressions for the MSL that are easy to interpret and compare with the baseline provided by the SPM bound. In Sec. 3.2.3 we will show how the PM estimator—the optimal choice—can achieve a better MSL, at the expense of having a more involved expression.

The MSL of the PGM can be computed from Eq. (14), by first evaluating the operators in Eqs. (17) as

MPGM,i\displaystyle M_{\text{PGM},i} =ρ0−12​ρ¯i​ρ0−12,\displaystyle=\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bar{\rho}_{i}\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, (29a)
MPGM,i​j\displaystyle M_{\text{PGM},{ij}} =ρ0−12​[∫d​~​𝜽​p​(~​𝜽)​ρ​(~​𝜽)​θ~i​θ~j]​ρ0−12.\displaystyle=\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left[\int\!\mathrm{d}\tilde{}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\tilde{}\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho(\tilde{}\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\tilde{\theta}_{i}\tilde{\theta}_{j}\right]\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}. (29b)

Noticing that, from cyclicity of the trace,

Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ0​MPGM,j​i]=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝜽T​L​𝜽=λ,L^{ij}\Tr[\rho_{0}\,M_{\text{PGM},{ji}}]=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}L\,\boldsymbol{\theta}=\lambda, (30)

since ρ0\rho_{0} is cancelled by the two factors ρ0−12\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}} and Tr⁡[ρ⁡(𝜽~)]=1\Tr[\rho(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}})]=1, we obtain

ℒPGM\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}} =2​(λ−Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ¯j​ρ0−12​ρ¯i​ρ0−12])\displaystyle=2\left(\lambda-L^{ij}\Tr\left[\bar{\rho}_{j}\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bar{\rho}_{i}\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right]\right) (31)
=2​(λ−Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ¯j​Eρ0,sq−1​[ρ¯i]]).\displaystyle=2\left(\lambda-L^{ij}\Tr\left[\bar{\rho}_{j}E_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{sq}}^{-1}[\bar{\rho}_{i}]\right]\right)\,.

In the second line, we have expressed the MSL in terms of the inverse of the map

Eρ,sq​[X]≔ρ​X​ρ.E_{\rho,\mathrm{sq}}[X]\coloneq\sqrt{\rho}X\sqrt{\rho}. (32)

This map, like Eρ,SE_{\rho,S} in Eq. (23), is one of the infinitely many inequivalent ways of introducing a superoperator representing “multiplication by ρ\rho”. This plurality is due to noncommutativity in quantum theory, and indeed for diagonal ρ\rho and XX, i.e., embedding classical probability into quantum objects, they all correspond to an element-wise multiplication of probability vectors. Such maps are fundamental mathematical objects in the theory of monotone metrics [136, 112, 137].

3.2.2 Fundamental incompatibility upper bound

A crucial result for us in the theory of monotone metrics is that the inner product obtained from the inverse of EρSE_{\rho}^{S} is the minimal one, implying the inequality

Tr⁡(X​Eρ,S−1​[X])≤Tr⁡(X​Eρ,sq−1​[X]).\Tr(XE_{\rho,\mathrm{S}}^{-1}\left[X\right])\leq\Tr(XE_{\rho,\mathrm{sq}}^{-1}\left[X\right])\,. (33)

Notice that the two sides of the inequality are norms induced by different inner products between operators. Since the weight matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, it admits a (non-unique) decomposition as a sum of rank-one outer products: L=∑k𝒗k​𝒗kTL=\sum_{k}\boldsymbol{v}_{k}\boldsymbol{v}_{k}^{T} for some real vectors 𝒗k\boldsymbol{v}_{k}. This, together with linearity of Eρ0,sq−1E_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{sq}}^{-1}, allows to rewrite the second term of Eq. (31) as the sum of norms of the Hermitian operators vki​ρ¯iv_{k}^{i}\bar{\rho}_{i}:

Li​jTr[ρ¯jEρ0,sq−1[ρ¯i]]=∑kTr⁡[(vki​ρ¯i)​Eρ0,sq−1​[(vkj​ρ¯j)]].\begin{split}L^{ij}\Tr\left[\bar{\rho}_{j}E_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{sq}}^{-1}[\bar{\rho}_{i}]\right]=\sum_{k}&\Tr\left[(v_{k}^{i}\bar{\rho}_{i})E_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{sq}}^{-1}[(v_{k}^{j}\bar{\rho}_{j})]\right].\end{split} (34)

Plugging this identity into the second term of Eq. (31) and applying the inequality (33) to each summand, we prove the first inequality in the following chain

2​ℒSPM≥ℒPGM≥ℒmin≥ℒSPM,2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}, (35)

where the second inequality holds by definition and the third is the SPM lower bound in Eq. (21), which neglects potential incompatibility effects. Thus, we have succeeded in bounding the maximal increase in the MSL due to measurement incompatibility, which can equivalently be written as an upper bound on the incompatibility figure of merit:

0≤ℐ≤1.0\leq\mathcal{I}\leq 1. (36)

We remark that the upper bound in Eq. (35) is our second and one of our key results. Interestingly, this mirrors a well-known result in local QET: the HCRB is at most twice the Helstrom (SLD) CRB [78, 79]. Notice, however, that the HCRB is in general attainable only asymptotically with collective measurements on multiple copies. Hence, only the fundamental asymptotic impact of measurement incompatibility is limited by the upper bound on the HCRB [64, 93]. On the other hand, our result is obtained in a Bayesian estimation setting, and holds for a single shot.

3.2.3 Pretty good measurement with optimal estimator

While generally valid, the bounds derived above can be trivial, i.e., less informative than the a priori MSL (cf. App. A): ℒprior≤ℒPGM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}\leq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}}, where

ℒprior=λ−𝝁T​L​𝝁,μi=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​θi.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}=\lambda-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{T}\,L\,\boldsymbol{\mu},\quad\mu_{i}=\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{i}. (37)

Such a behaviour may appear counter-intuitive, since measuring a system is supposed to increase the information about the parameters’ values. The intuition is re-established if one realises that this happens only because of a suboptimal choice of the classical estimator in the construction of the PGM bound. Similar situations may appear also in quantum state discrimination, i.e., for discrete hypotheses. Indeed, it has been shown that, for specific ensembles, guessing the hypothesis that maximises the prior probability is optimal and the probability of success cannot be improved upon by performing measurements on the system [138, 139].

Instead of viewing the PGM as a POVM already equipped with a built-in estimator—one not specifically tailored to our quadratic loss function—we now drop the interpretation of its outcomes as estimates. For clarity, the POVM elements in Eq. (28) can be rewritten with a distinct label for the measurement outcomes as

MPGM​(𝒙)=p⁡(𝒙)​ρ0−12​ρ​(𝒙)​ρ0−12,M_{\mathrm{PGM}}(\boldsymbol{x})=p(\boldsymbol{x})\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\rho(\boldsymbol{x})\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, (38)

where each 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} is still a vector in the hypothesis space Ω\Omega, though it is not directly used as an estimator. Instead, the measurement outcomes are processed through the optimal PM estimator in Eq. (26), which is constructed from the likelihood function p⁡(𝒙|𝜽)=Tr⁡[ρ⁡(𝜽)​MPGM​(𝒙)]p(\boldsymbol{x}|\boldsymbol{\theta})=\Tr[\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,M_{\mathrm{PGM}}(\boldsymbol{x})]. From a straightforward calculation, we obtain the MSL

ℒPGM∗≔λ−Li​j​∫𝒅𝒙p⁡(𝒙)​Tr⁡[ρ⁡(𝒙)​ρ0−12​ρ¯j​ρ0−12]⋅Tr⁡[ρ⁡(𝒙)​ρ0−12​ρ¯i​ρ0−12].\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}^{*}}\coloneq\lambda-L^{ij}\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}\,&p(\boldsymbol{x})\,\Tr\left[\rho(\boldsymbol{x})\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bar{\rho}_{j}\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right]\\ &\cdot\Tr\left[\rho(\boldsymbol{x})\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bar{\rho}_{i}\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right].\end{split} (39)

Contrary to the standard PGM, this quantity is guaranteed to be no greater than ℒprior\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}, which can be seen explicitly by applying Jensen’s inequality to the second term of Eq. (39), since the function of ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is quadratic and convex. Whilst for an arbitrary POVM with the same estimator—which is guaranteed to be smaller than ℒprior\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}—the MSL may be larger than ℒPGM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}}. Note that, as discussed, for our choice of quadratic loss we have a formal guarantee that the PM is the optimal classical estimator, but there is numerical evidence that it also leads to a better fidelity than the standard PGM approach in state estimation [140].

Tightening the previous inequalities, by taking into account that they may be trivial, and adding this new tighter upper bound, we obtain

min⁡[2​ℒSPM,ℒprior]\displaystyle\min\!\left[2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}},\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}\right] ≥min⁡[ℒPGM,ℒprior]\displaystyle\geq\min\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}},\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}\right] (40)
≥ℒPGM∗\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}^{*}}
≥ℒmin\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}
≥ℒSPM.\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}\,.

The corresponding bounds on ℐ\mathcal{I} are

0\displaystyle 0 ≤ℐ\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{I} (41)
≤ℐPGM∗\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM}^{*}}
≤min⁡[ℐPGM,ℐprior]\displaystyle\leq\min\!\left[\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM}},\,\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{prior}}\right]
≤min⁡[1,ℐprior],\displaystyle\leq\min\!\left[1,\,\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{prior}}\right],

where ℐPGM\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM}}, ℐPGM∗\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM^{*}}}, and ℐprior\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{prior}} are defined as in Eq. (27). The first three inequalities in Eq. (40) (the last three inequalities in Eq. (41)) constitute our third result.

3.3 Lower bounds

Having established an upper bound on the MSL to characterise the worst-case impact of measurement incompatibility, as well as a tighter version, our aim is now to tighten the lower bound in Eq. (36) for a given model. To this end, we seek lower bounds on the MSL that are tighter than ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}} in the presence of non-commuting SPM operators. In this section, we focus primarily on the tightest known lower bound on the MSL available in the literature, the Nagaoka–Hayashi (NH) bound, ℒNH\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}, recently introduced in Bayesian QET by Suzuki [104].

3.3.1 Nagaoka–Hayashi bound

To derive this bound, one starts by noticing that any choice of POVM and estimators satisfies the following inequality [104, Lemma 1],

∑i​j|i⟩​⟨j|⊗Mi​j⪰∑i​j|i⟩​⟨j|⊗Mi​Mj,\sum_{ij}|i\rangle\langle j|\otimes M_{ij}\succeq\sum_{ij}|i\rangle\langle j|\otimes M_{i}M_{j}\,, (42)

in terms of the first and second moment operators introduced in Eq. (17). Note that an additional vector space of dimension dd (number of parameters) has been introduced, but this is not a physical Hilbert space. While we use the bra–ket notation, |k⟩\ket{k} simply stands for the standard column basis vector eke_{k} of ℝd\mathbbm{R}^{d} (we have also temporarily reintroduced an explicit summation for extra clarity). The two sides of Eq. (42) are block matrices: the left-hand side can be interpreted as an operator-valued second moment matrix, while the right-hand side as an outer product of operator-valued first moment vectors.

Since the MSL in Eq. (14) is expressed only in terms of these operators, a lower bound is obtained by treating the Hermitian operators Mi​j=Mj​iM_{ij}=M_{ji} and MiM_{i} as independent variables satisfying Eq. (42):

ℒNH≔λ+\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}\coloneq\lambda+ min{Mi​j,Mi}⁡Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ0​Mj​i−2​ρ¯j​Mi]\displaystyle\min_{\{M_{ij},M_{i}\}}L^{ij}\,\operatorname{Tr}[\rho_{0}M_{ji}-2\bar{\rho}_{j}M_{i}] (43)
subject​to​Eq.(42).\displaystyle\,\,\mathrm{subject\penalty\ to\penalty\ }\mathrm{Eq.\penalty\ }\eqref{eq:lemma1-Suzuki}\,.

This means that, for a given set of Mi​jM_{ij} and MiM_{i} attaining the minimum, there is no guarantee that an underlying POVM M⁡(x)M(x) exists from which they can be derived, according to Eqs. (17). Consequently, the bound may be loose. However, despite not fully capturing measurement incompatibility, the NH bound can be shown to be tighter than the SPM one. This follows by noticing that Eq. (42) implies

Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ0​Mj​i]≥Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ0​Mj​Mi],L^{ij}\Tr[\rho_{0}M_{ji}]\geq L^{ij}\Tr[\rho_{0}M_{j}M_{i}], (44)

which is a weaker constraint. Applying this inequality to Eq. (43) one obtains a relaxation of the original problem that can be solved analytically to obtain ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}.

The bound ℒNH\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}} formally mirrors the NH Cramér-Rao bound (NHCRB) in local QET [90], and analogously it can be evaluated by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) [104]. Notice, however, that the upper bound in Eq. (35) that holds in the Bayesian case has no direct counterpart in the local case, since the NHCRB can be much larger than twice the Helstrom (SLD) CRB, and this gap can grow with the dimension of the Hilbert space and number of parameters [93].

For two parameters, the optimisation over the second moment operators M11M_{11}, M12M_{12} and M22M_{22} can be solved exactly. For the sake of clarity, but without loss of generality44 4 Similarly to local QET, the scalar NH bound can be recast to an equivalent problem with L=𝕀L=\mathbb{I} and suitably redefined first moment operators ρ¯i′=∑j(L)i​j​ρ¯j\bar{\rho}_{i}^{\prime}=\sum_{j}(\sqrt{L})^{ij}\bar{\rho}_{j}. The explicit expression for a general weight matrix is also reported in Ref. [104, Eq. (20)]., we present this expression for an identity weight matrix:

ℒNH=L=𝕀2λ+minM1,M2{Tr[ρ0(M12+M22)]+‖ρ0[M1,M2]ρ0‖1−2Tr[ρ¯1M1+ρ¯2M2]},\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}\overset{L=\mathbb{I}_{2}}{=}\lambda+\min_{M_{1},M_{2}}\{\Tr\left[\rho_{0}(M_{1}^{2}+M_{2}^{2})\right]\\ +\left\|\sqrt{\rho_{0}}[M_{1},M_{2}]\sqrt{\rho_{0}}\right\|_{1}-2\Tr\left[\bar{\rho}_{1}M_{1}+\bar{\rho}_{2}M_{2}\right]\}\,,\end{split} (45)

where ‖A‖1=Tr⁡[A†​A]\|A\|_{1}=\Tr[\sqrt{A^{\dagger}A}] denotes the trace norm, i.e., the sum of the singular values. This expression can be derived from Eq. (43), following, e.g., Ref. [90, Supplementary Note 2]. This form is the one originally obtained by Nagaoka for local two-parameter estimation [87].

Further considering a single qubit and full-rank ρ0\rho_{0} (the only nontrivial qubit case), the NH bound in Eq. (45) is in fact attainable, i.e., ℒNH=ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}, because Nagaoka’s argument carries over to the Bayesian setting; we show this in App. C. The proof is constructive and yields an explicit optimal POVM, reported in App. C.1. Moreover, this case can be solved in closed form: the remaining optimisation over M1,M2M_{1},M_{2} in Eq. (45) is evaluated in App. C.2.

Overall, we have the following inequalities:

ℒmin≥ℒNH≥ℒSPM.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}\,. (46)

In turn, this restricts the allowed range of the incompatibility figure of merit for a given model:

ℐNH≤ℐ≤1,\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{NH}}\leq\mathcal{I}\leq 1\,, (47)

where ℐNH\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{NH}} is defined analogously to Eq. (27). Moreover, by combining this NH bound on incompatibility with the tightest upper bound in Eq. (40), we obtain a tight range for the possible values of incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation:

ℐNH≤ℐ≤ℐPGM∗.\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{NH}}\leq\mathcal{I}\leq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM}^{*}}. (48)

This constitutes our fourth result.

3.3.2 Other lower bounds

We conclude this section by highlighting other lower bounds on the MSL which, although less tight—and mostly derived using techniques from local QET—can be easier to compute and may therefore remain useful in practice.

We first mention the Holevo bound, here denoted as ℒH\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H}}, which is a Bayesian version of the HCRB [104, 105]. It can be obtained by loosening the constraints in Eq. (42) taking the expectation value with respect to ρ0\rho_{0}, thereby obtaining a minimisation problem with an inequality constraint involving d×dd{\times}d matrices. The HCRB sits between the SPM and NH bounds: ℒNH≥ℒH≥ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}. While in local QET the HCRB has a fundamental meaning, being asymptotically attainable, the Bayesian version does not seem to share the same significance55 5 Note that such a Bayesian Holevo-type bound is different from the so-called Bayesian CRBs obtained by averaging the HCRB over the prior [141], conjectured to be attainable in the large sample limit of Bayesian estimation [10, Sec. 5.5]; see the discussion in Sec. 5.. The Bayesian Holevo bound may be computationally more efficient because, while it can be computed by solving an SDP as the NH bound, it involves positive semidefinite constraints in terms of matrices of smaller dimension [104].

Pursuing further the goal of identifying easily computable bounds, one may instead seek lower bounds that capture measurement incompatibility to some extent and can always be expressed in closed form, rather than indirectly as the outcome of an optimisation. A whole class of such bounds exists, based on the idea of non-commutative PM operators, of which SPMs are just one example. This is in full analogy with logarithmic derivative operators in local QET [112, Ch. 6]. In App. D, we derive this family of lower bounds in a unified manner, employing the theory of monotone metrics, and generalising the approach of Ref. [43]. Here, we only mention the right posterior mean (RPM) bound

ℒRPM\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RPM}} ≔λ−Li​j​𝒦R,j​i+‖L​Im⁡[𝒦R]​L‖1,\displaystyle\coloneq\lambda-L^{ij}\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{R},ji}+\|\sqrt{L}\Im[\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{R}}]\sqrt{L}\|_{1}, (49a)
𝒦R,i​j\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{R},ij} ≔Tr⁡[ρ¯i​ρ0−1​ρ¯j],\displaystyle\coloneq\Tr[\bar{\rho}_{i}\rho_{0}^{-1}\bar{\rho}_{j}], (49b)

written in terms of the complex matrix 𝒦R\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{R}}. Such a matrix is analogous to the right logarithmic derivative quantum Fisher information matrix in local QET. This bound is less informative than the NH or Holevo ones, since ℒH≥ℒRPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RPM}} [105, Thm. 8]. However, it can be tighter or looser than ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}} depending on the specific model. For example, it is always less tight than the SPM bound for d=1d=1, where the latter is attainable. Conversely, Holevo has shown the RPM bound to be attainable for a multiparameter problem with non-commuting SPM operators: estimation of the average position and momentum of a Gaussian state with a Gaussian prior [127].

As a means of summary, we combine the upper bounds in Eq. (40) with all the lower bounds discussed in this section to obtain the following hierarchy of bounds on the minimum MSL:

min⁡[2​ℒSPM,ℒprior]\displaystyle\min\!\left[2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}},\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}\right] ≥min⁡[ℒPGM,ℒprior]\displaystyle\geq\min\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}},\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}\right] (50)
≥ℒPGM∗\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}^{*}}
≥ℒmin\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}
≥ℒNH\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}
≥ℒH\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H}}
≥max⁡[ℒSPM,ℒRPM].\displaystyle\geq\max\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}},\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RPM}}\right].

Correspondingly, the hierarchy of bounds on measurement incompatibility is

max⁡[0,ℐRPM]\displaystyle\max\!\left[0,\,\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{RPM}}\right] ≤ℐH\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{H}} (51)
≤ℐNH\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{NH}}
≤ℐ\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{I}
≤ℐPGM∗\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM}^{*}}
≤min⁡[ℐPGM,ℐprior]\displaystyle\leq\min\!\left[\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM}},\,\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{prior}}\right]
≤min⁡[1,ℐprior],\displaystyle\leq\min\!\left[1,\,\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{prior}}\right],

where ℐRPM\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{RPM}} and ℐH\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{H}} are defined as in Eq. (27).

3.4 Approaching the minimum MSL numerically

While the bounds derived above enable efficient estimation of the incompatibility range, the exact value of the minimum MSL ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\min} typically requires numerical optimisation over POVMs. A practical approach, introduced in Ref. [107] in the more general setting of channel estimation, is an iterative see-saw (alternating optimisation) method. Here, we briefly summarise the variant relevant to our setting of parameter-dependent families of states.

We restrict, without loss of generality, to POVMs with a finite number of outcomes, denoted as {Mn}n=1N\{M_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}; see the definition in Eq. (4), with associated estimator values {𝜽~n}n=1N\{\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}. For the quadratic loss in Eq. (10)—or its symmetry-remapped version in Eq. (13)—the MSL can be written as a constant term depending only on the prior moments plus a term that is linear in the POVM elements for fixed estimators. Concretely, defining θ~n,i\tilde{\theta}_{n,i} as the ii-th component of the estimator associated with outcome nn, one can rewrite

ℒ=λ−∑n=1NTr⁡[Mn​Xn​(𝜽~n)],\mathcal{L}=\lambda-\sum_{n=1}^{N}\Tr\!\big[M_{n}\,X_{n}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}_{n})\big], (52)

where each Xn​(𝜽~n)X_{n}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}_{n}) is a Hermitian operator that depends only on the zeroth and first state moments ρ0\rho_{0} and {ρ¯i}\{\bar{\rho}_{i}\} in Eqs. (16a) and (16b), and on the weight matrix LL. The explicit expression is obtained by inserting the definition of the measurement moments for a discrete-outcome POVM Mi=∑nθ~n,i​MnM_{i}=\sum_{n}\tilde{\theta}_{n,i}M_{n} and Mi​j=∑nθ~n,i​θ~n,j​MnM_{ij}=\sum_{n}\tilde{\theta}_{n,i}\tilde{\theta}_{n,j}M_{n} into Eq. (14), which yields

Xn​(𝜽~n)=2​Li​j​θ~n,i​ρ¯j−Li​j​θ~n,i​θ~n,j​ρ0.X_{n}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{n})=2\,L^{ij}\,\tilde{\theta}_{n,i}\,\bar{\rho}_{j}-L^{ij}\,\tilde{\theta}_{n,i}\tilde{\theta}_{n,j}\,\rho_{0}. (53)

Therefore, for fixed {𝜽~n(t)}\{\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}_{n}^{(t)}\}, where tt labels each iteration, the optimisation over the measurement reduces to a SDP:

max⁡∑n=1N{Mn}⁡Tr⁡[Mn​Xn​(𝜽~n(t))]s.t.Mn⪰0,∑n=1NMn=𝕀.\max_{\{M_{n}\}}\;\sum_{n=1}^{N}\Tr\!\big[M_{n}\,X_{n}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{n}^{(t)})\big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad M_{n}\succeq 0,\ \sum_{n=1}^{N}M_{n}=\mathbb{I}. (54)

This step is convex and can be solved to global optimality for the chosen number of outcomes NN. For a DD-dimensional system, at most N=D2N=D^{2} outcomes are needed [107].

For fixed POVM {Mn(t)}\{M_{n}^{(t)}\}, obtained by solving the SDP above, the optimal classical post-processing for quadratic loss is the PM estimator in Eq. (11) and no optimisation is needed; for different loss functions, a second optimisation is generally needed [107]. In our notation, this update can be expressed directly in terms of the state moments:

θ~n,i(t+1)=Tr⁡[Mn(t)​ρ¯i]Tr⁡[Mn(t)​ρ0],\tilde{\theta}_{n,i}^{(t+1)}=\frac{\Tr\!\big[M_{n}^{(t)}\,\bar{\rho}_{i}\big]}{\Tr\!\big[M_{n}^{(t)}\,\rho_{0}\big]}, (55)

and analogously after the symmetry remapping 𝜽↦𝒇⁡(𝜽)\boldsymbol{\theta}\mapsto\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\theta}).

Iterating Eqs. (54) and (55) yields a sequence of feasible strategies whose MSL is non-increasing at every step. The procedure is not guaranteed to find the global optimum in general—the joint optimisation over POVMs and estimators is non-convex—but in practice it provides a constructive upper bound on ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\min}. To mitigate the risk of converging to suboptimal stationary points, one may perform multiple random initialisations of the estimators and keep the best solution. Finally, candidate solutions produced by the see-saw could also be checked against the optimality conditions in Eq. (19), providing an a posteriori consistency test.

This gives (as any POVM would) an upper bound on incompatibility (ℐSSW\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{SSW}}). However, iteratively solving the SDPs is an additional layer of computational complexity, potentially requiring a scaling—in the number of POVM elements to solve for—with the square of the state-space dimension.

4 Applications

In the following sections we evaluate the measurement incompatibility range in Eq. (48), as well as some of the less tight bounds derived, for a range of examples.

4.1 Discrete quantum phase imaging

Consider a (d+1)(d{+}1)-mode interferometer, where dd parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} for a set of unknown phases 𝚯\boldsymbol{\Theta} are encoded via the unitary operator e−i​Nj​θj\mathrm{e}^{-iN^{j}\theta_{j}}. Here, NjN^{j} is the number operator of the jjth mode, and the zeroth mode serves as a reference beam [142]. This configuration models discrete quantum imaging and has been extensively explored in both local and Bayesian frameworks [143, 41, 67, 43, 144]. In this context, a common probe state is the nn-photon generalised N00N state

|ψ⁡(θ)⟩=1d+α2​(α​e−i​n​θ0​|n0⟩+∑i=1de−i​n​θi​|ni⟩),\ket{\psi(\theta)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d+\alpha^{2}}}\left(\alpha e^{-in\theta_{0}}\ket{n_{0}}+\sum_{i=1}^{d}e^{-in\theta_{i}}\ket{n_{i}}\right), (56)

with α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} and

|ni⟩:=|0⟩0⊗⋯⊗|0⟩i−1⊗|n⟩i⊗|0⟩i+1⊗⋯⊗|0⟩d\ket{n_{i}}:=\ket{0}_{0}\otimes\cdots\otimes\ket{0}_{i-1}\otimes\ket{n}_{i}\otimes\ket{0}_{i+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\ket{0}_{d} (57)

representing a state with nn photons in the ii-th mode, such that ∑jNj​|ψ⁡(θ)⟩=n​|ψ⁡(θ)⟩\sum\limits_{j}N^{j}\ket{\psi(\theta)}=n\ket{\psi(\theta)}.

To address this problem using the MSL, we restrict the hypothesis space Ω\Omega so that the phases are sufficiently localised to behave as location parameters, but remaining within a global regime. Specifically, we employ a flat prior p⁡(𝜽)=(n2​π)dp(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\left(\frac{n}{2\pi}\right)^{d}, with θi∈[−π/n,π/n]\theta_{i}\in[-\pi/n,\pi/n] and n≥4n\geq 4, so that the largest prior width for the ii-th parameter is π/2\pi/2. For this configuration—and choosing a normalised LL with equal weights, i.e., L=𝕀/dL=\mathbb{I}/d—the average state, SPM operators, and SPM bound are, respectively [13],

ρ0=1d+α2​(α2​|n0⟩​⟨n0|+∑i=1d|ni⟩​⟨ni|),\displaystyle\rho_{0}=\frac{1}{d+\alpha^{2}}\left(\alpha^{2}\ket{n_{0}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{0}}}+\sum_{i=1}^{d}\ket{n_{i}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{i}}}\right), (58)
ρ¯j=−i​αn⁡(d+α2)​(|nj⟩​⟨n0|−|n0⟩​⟨nj|),\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{j}=\frac{-i\alpha}{n(d+\alpha^{2})}\left(\ket{n_{j}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{0}}}-\ket{n_{0}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{j}}}\right), (59)
Sj=−2​i​αn⁡(1+α2)​(|nj⟩​⟨n0|−|n0⟩​⟨nj|),\displaystyle S_{j}=\frac{-2i\alpha}{n(1+\alpha^{2})}\left(\ket{n_{j}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{0}}}-\ket{n_{0}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{j}}}\right), (60)

and

ℒSPM=1n2​[π23−4​α2(1+α2)​(d+α2)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}-\frac{4\alpha^{2}}{(1+\alpha^{2})(d+\alpha^{2})}\right]. (61)

Two observations are in order. First, the Heisenberg scaling in Eq. (61) is achievable in a global setting only because the chosen prior width scales as ∼​1/n\mathord{\sim}1/n. Indeed, since all first moments of the prior vanish for this problem, the a priori MSL is given by (cf. Eq. (37))

ℒprior=λ=π23​n2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}=\lambda=\frac{\pi^{2}}{3n^{2}}, (62)

which already exhibits Heisenberg scaling; this is consistent with the observations in Refs. [145, 146, 12, 40, 147, 148].

Secondly, and more importantly for our purposes, the SPM operators do not commute:

[Sj,Sk]=4​α2n2​(1+α2)2​(|nj⟩​⟨nk|−|nk⟩​⟨nj|).[S_{j},S_{k}]=\frac{4\alpha^{2}}{n^{2}(1+\alpha^{2})^{2}}(\ket{n_{j}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{k}}}-\ket{n_{k}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{j}}}). (63)

As such, the SPM bound is not tight, and we can therefore expect incompatibility to arise in this system.

To quantify the amount of incompatibility, we first need to calculate the bounds on the minimum MSL. We start with the PGM bound, given in Eq. (31). Since

ρ¯j​ρ0−12=−in​d+α2​(|nj⟩​⟨n0|−α​|n0⟩​⟨nj|),\bar{\rho}_{j}\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{-i}{n\sqrt{d+\alpha^{2}}}\left(\ket{n_{j}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{0}}}-\alpha\ket{n_{0}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{j}}}\right), (64)

and so

Tr⁡[ρ¯j​ρ0−12​ρ¯i​ρ0−12]=2​αn2​(d+α2)​δj​i,\Tr[\bar{\rho}_{j}\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\bar{\rho}_{i}\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}]=\frac{2\alpha}{n^{2}(d+\alpha^{2})}\delta_{ji}, (65)

Eq. (31) yields

ℒPGM=2n2​(π23−2​αd+α2).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}}=\frac{2}{n^{2}}\left(\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}-\frac{2\alpha}{d+\alpha^{2}}\right). (66)

However, this upper bound is trivial, i.e., ℒPGM>ℒprior\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}}>\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}, and consequently so is 2​ℒSPM2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}. This follows from showing that ℒPGM−ℒprior\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}}-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}} is strictly positive by virtue of the inequality

π23>maxα⁡4​αd+α2=2d,\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}>\max_{\alpha}\frac{4\alpha}{d+\alpha^{2}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}}, (67)

valid for all dd.

In view of this, we proceed to calculate the PGM bound enhanced by the PM estimator, given in Eq. (39), which is guaranteed to be smaller than or equal to the a priori MSL. First, calculate

ρ0−12​ρ¯j​ρ0−12=in​(|n0⟩​⟨nj|−|nj⟩​⟨n0|),\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\bar{\rho}_{j}\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{i}{n}(\ket{n_{0}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{j}}}-\ket{n_{j}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{0}}}), (68)

so that

Tr⁡[ρ⁡(𝜽)​ρ0−12​ρ¯j​ρ0−12]=2​α​sin⁡(n​θj)n⁡(d+α2).\Tr[\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\bar{\rho}_{j}\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}]=\frac{2\alpha\sin(n\theta_{j})}{n(d+\alpha^{2})}. (69)

Since the following integrals hold:

∫−π/nπ/ndθjsin(nθj)=0,∫−π/nπ/ndθjsin2(nθj)=πn,\int\limits_{-\pi/n}^{\pi/n}\mathrm{d}\theta_{j}\,\sin(n\theta_{j})=0,\!\int\limits_{-\pi/n}^{\pi/n}\mathrm{d}\theta_{j}\,\sin^{2}(n\theta_{j})=\frac{\pi}{n}, (70)

Eq. (39) leads to

ℒPGM∗=1n2​(π23−2​α2(d+α2)2).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}^{*}}=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left(\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}-\frac{2\alpha^{2}}{\left(d+\alpha^{2}\right)^{2}}\right). (71)

This is our tightest upper bound on the minimum MSL.

We next turn to the lower bounds. We begin with the simplest tractable bound beyond the SPM bound, namely the RPM bound in Eq. (49a). Using

ρ¯j​ρ0−1​ρ¯k=1n2​(d+α2)​(|nj⟩​⟨nk|+α2​δj​k​|n0⟩​⟨n0|),\bar{\rho}_{j}\,\rho_{0}^{-1}\,\bar{\rho}_{k}=\frac{1}{n^{2}(d+\alpha^{2})}\left(\ket{n_{j}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{k}}}+\alpha^{2}\delta_{jk}\ket{n_{0}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{0}}}\right), (72)

we obtain

𝒦R,j​k=1+α2n2​(d+α2)​δj​k,\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{R},jk}=\frac{1+\alpha^{2}}{n^{2}(d+\alpha^{2})}\,\delta_{jk}, (73)

and therefore

ℒRPM=1n2​(π23−1+α2d+α2).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RPM}}=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left(\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}-\frac{1+\alpha^{2}}{d+\alpha^{2}}\right). (74)

However, it is straightforward to verify that ℒSPM≥ℒRPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RPM}}, consistent with the fact that 𝒦R\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{R}} in Eq. (73) is real-valued. Consequently, we shall instead evaluate the NH bound in Eq. (43) using the numerical algorithm of Ref. [113] to obtain a tighter lower bound on the minimum MSL.

We are now in a position to quantify measurement incompatibility. Building on the preceding results, Fig. 1 illustrates as a shaded region the range defined in Eq. (48), showing its dependence on the number of parameters dd and using the state with α=d1/4\alpha=d^{1/4} that minimises Eq. (61). The upper boundary of this region is given by ℐPGM∗\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM^{*}}} (dashed-dot line), while the lower boundary corresponds to ℐNH\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{NH}} (solid line). For comparison, we also include the incompatibility quantifier associated with the a priori MSL (dotted line) and the PGM bound (dashed line). As can be seen, the latter exceeds the former and is therefore trivial, as discussed above. Finally, the reference value ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}} is shown in the first inset, likewise plotted as a function of dd.

Fig. 1 confirms the presence of measurement incompatibility within this protocol, with values not exceeding 0.20.2. This relatively low magnitude can initially be attributed to the proximity between ℒprior\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}} and ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}, evidenced by the dotted line. That is, within the Bayesian framework, the prior information imposes a finite and natural upper bound on the MSL, thereby limiting the maximum attainable relative precision gain. This effect becomes especially evident as the number of parameters increases, leading to a progressive reduction in relative precision gain and leaving increasingly limited scope for incompatibility to exert a noticeable influence on the precision. Nevertheless, the second inset demonstrates that the protocol consistently exhibits a nonzero degree of measurement incompatibility.

Here we see a deviation from the results for this model in local QET [41, 132], where the SLD bound is attainable—and no incompatibility is seen—due to the commuting generators which give rise to commuting SLD operators for pure state probes. With pure states leading to a mixed-state quantum statistical model in the Bayesian framework, the corresponding SPM operators do not directly commute and incompatibility is found as the SPM bound is unobtainable. Nevertheless that incompatibility is small, and numerical evidence using the method described in Sec. 3.4 suggests it is at the lower end of the incompatibility window shown in Fig. 1 as the NH bound appears attainable with |ℐNH−ℐSSW|≤3×10−4\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{NH}}-\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{SSW}}\rvert\leq 3{\times}10^{-4} for 2≤d≤102\leq d\leq 10 [149].

Symmetries, including the commuting generators, of the physical configuration may yet be responsible for both the low incompatibility, and apparent numeric saturability of the NH bound. It is perhaps informative to note that, while lacking the operational meaning it has in local QET [124], a Bayesian analogue of the so-called weak commutativity,

Tr⁡[ρ0​[Sj,Sk]]=0,\Tr\left[\rho_{0}[S_{j},S_{k}]\right]=0, (75)

does still hold in this case, since

ρ0​[Sj,Sk]=4​α2n2​(1+α2)2​(d+α2)​(|nj⟩​⟨nk|−|nk⟩​⟨nj|).\rho_{0}[S_{j},S_{k}]=\frac{4\alpha^{2}}{n^{2}(1+\alpha^{2})^{2}(d+\alpha^{2})}\bigl(\ket{n_{j}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{k}}}-\ket{n_{k}}\mkern-4.0mu{\bra{n_{j}}}\bigr). (76)

4.2 Phase and dephasing estimation

While phase estimation serves as the archetypal problem in quantum estimation, the simultaneous estimation of phase and phase diffusion plays an analogous role in multiparameter quantum estimation. The simplest single-qubit incarnation of this model exhibits measurement incompatibility in local QET [150], which however asymptotically disappears as many identical copies are measured collectively [151]. This corresponds to preparing identical and factorised probe states, whereas asymptotically large entangled probes generally allow to optimally estimate both parameters [152]. Nevertheless, we consider here independent identical copies collectively measured, since this is a paradigmatic setting for investigating measurement incompatibility [150, 151, 153].

For an initial state ρin\rho_{\mathrm{in}}, the single-qubit phase and phase-diffusion channels66 6 The qubit can represent, e.g., a single-photon in optical interferometry, whereas the same setup for probe states with more photons is not equivalent to considering multiple copies of the single-photon state, but give rise to correlated dephasing [154, 155]., which commute, are defined as

Λ1​(ρin)\displaystyle\Lambda_{1}(\rho_{\mathrm{in}}) =e−i​θ12​σz​ρin​ei​θ12​σz,\displaystyle=\mathrm{e}^{-i\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\sigma_{z}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm{e}^{i\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\sigma_{z}}, (77a)
Λ2​(ρin)\displaystyle\Lambda_{2}(\rho_{\mathrm{in}}) =∫−∞∞d​x​e−x24​θ222​π​θ2​e−i​x2​σz​ρin​ei​x2​σz,\displaystyle=\int\limits_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}x\,\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{4\theta_{2}^{2}}}}{2\sqrt{\pi}\,\theta_{2}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-i\frac{x}{2}\sigma_{z}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm{e}^{i\frac{x}{2}\sigma_{z}}, (77b)

respectively; σx\sigma_{x}, σy\sigma_{y} and σz\sigma_{z} denote Pauli matrices. The corresponding parameter-dependent state is

ρ⁡(𝜽)=12​(𝕀2+cos⁡θ1​e−θ22​σx−sin⁡θ1​e−θ22​σy).\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{2}(\mathbb{I}_{2}+\cos\theta_{1}\mathrm{e}^{-\theta_{2}^{2}}\sigma_{x}-\sin\theta_{1}\mathrm{e}^{-\theta_{2}^{2}}\sigma_{y})\,. (78)

The MSL is not suitable for this problem. Specifically, while θ1∈[−W12,W12]\theta_{1}\in[-\frac{W_{1}}{2},\frac{W_{1}}{2}] is a cyclic variable that can be treated as a location parameter when W1≲π/2W_{1}\lesssim\pi/2—see Sec. 2.2—θ2>0\theta_{2}>0 in Eq. (77b) is a scale parameter [47, 115], for which the appropriate loss function is logarithmic [133]. Consequently, one must employ a symmetry-informed loss function of the kind in Eq. (13).

A particular realisation, independently enforcing translation invariance for θ1\theta_{1} and scale invariance for θ2\theta_{2}, is given by

l⁡(𝜽~,𝜽)=(θ~1−θ1)2+log2⁡(θ~2θ2),l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta})=(\tilde{\theta}_{1}-\theta_{1})^{2}+\log^{2}\left(\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{2}}{\theta_{2}}\right), (79)

which mixes two uncertainty types [37]. Here, we assume L=𝕀2L=\mathbb{I}_{2}. This corresponds to using the multiparameter symmetry function

𝒇⁡(𝜽)=(f1​(𝜽)f2​(𝜽))=(θ1log⁡(θ2)).\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\begin{pmatrix}f_{1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\\ f_{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\theta_{1}\\ \log(\theta_{2})\end{pmatrix}. (80)

Crucially, given that Eq. (79) preserves the quadratic structure of the square loss (10), the bounds derived in this work remain unchanged, except for the definitions of the prior moments,

𝝁\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu} =∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝒇​(𝜽),\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), (81a)
λ\displaystyle\lambda =∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝒇​(𝜽)T​L​𝒇​(𝜽);\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{T}L\,\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\theta}); (81b)

the first state moments,

ρ¯i=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ρ​(𝜽)​fi​(𝜽);\bar{\rho}_{i}=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,f_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}); (82)

and the measurement moments,

Mi\displaystyle M_{i} =∫d​𝜽~​M​(𝜽~)​fi​(𝜽~),\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}\,M(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\,f_{i}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}), (83a)
