p⁡(θ1,θ2)=1θ2​W1​log⁡(W2)∝1θ2,p(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=\frac{1}{\theta_{2}W_{1}\log(W_{2})}\propto\frac{1}{\theta_{2}}, (84)

with θ1∈[−W1/2,W1/2]\theta_{1}\in[-W_{1}/2,\,W_{1}/2] and θ2∈[1/W2,W2]\theta_{2}\in[1/\sqrt{W_{2}},\,\sqrt{W_{2}}], for which the corresponding a priori MSL reads

ℒprior=λ=112​[W12+log2⁡(W2)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}=\lambda=\frac{1}{12}\left[W_{1}^{2}+\log^{2}(W_{2})\right]. (85)

Eq. (84) is the product of two independent priors—the first flat, representing maximum ignorance for a location, and the second Jeffreys’s prior, representing maximum ignorance for a scale [47, 115]. The range for the dephasing parameter takes such a form when a symmetric, flat range of width W2W_{2} is imposed in the log-transformed space.

Given this formulation, the state moments for a single copy can be calculated to have form

ρ0\displaystyle\rho_{0} =12​[𝕀2+g⁡(W1,W2)​σx],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}[\mathbb{I}_{2}+g(W_{1},W_{2})\,\sigma_{x}], (86a)
ρ¯1\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{1} ∝σy,\displaystyle\propto\sigma_{y}, (86b)
ρ¯2\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{2} ∝σx,\displaystyle\propto\sigma_{x}, (86c)

with the exact expressions given in App. E. Although this is a qubit system amenable to further analytic treatment, the resulting expressions are not very informative. For our purposes, it suffices to note that the SPM operators arising from Eqs. (183a) have the following structure:

S1\displaystyle S_{1} ∝σy,\displaystyle\propto\sigma_{y}, (87a)
S2\displaystyle S_{2} ∝𝕀2+h⁡(W1,W2)​σx.\displaystyle\propto\mathbb{I}_{2}+h(W_{1},W_{2})\,\sigma_{x}. (87b)

As can be observed, the SPM operators do not generally commute, thereby guaranteeing the presence of measurement incompatibility at the single-copy level. However, the Bayesian weak commutativity condition proposed in Eq. (75) does hold (as the weak commutativity condition does for the local setting [150]). This also holds for the many-copy version [149], which we consider next.

Let ρ⊗n​(𝜽)\rho^{\otimes n}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) be the nn-copy state. Due to the prior, the corresponding nn-copy average state and first moments, i.e., ∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ρ⊗n​(𝜽)\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho^{\otimes n}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and ∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ρ⊗n​(𝜽)​θj\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho^{\otimes n}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{j}, are not directly tensor powers of the single-copy ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ¯j\bar{\rho}_{j} in Eqs. (183a).

In lieu of the PGM enhanced by PM estimator bound (due to the high dimension of the nn-copy state), we consider a local qubit tomography—where each copy is measured at random in the basis of one of the three Pauli operators. The outcomes are then processed with the optimal PM estimator, such that the resulting MSL lower bounds ℒprior\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}, which is again the tighter bound than ℒPGM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}}.

In Fig. 2 we present numerical results on measurement incompatibility, by evaluating upper and lower bounds as a function of the number of copies, for prior widths W1=π/2W_{1}=\pi/2 and W2=5W_{2}=5. The main plot shows that the incompatibility window grows with the number of copies, with the incompatibility NH lower bound increasing slightly, and the tomography upper bound increasing more rapidly. The latter result may be expected, since tomography corresponds to measuring each copy separately and thus cannot take advantage of collective effects.

Interestingly, the overall behaviour appears to be qualitatively different from local QET, where the initially large incompatibility decreases by measuring multiple copies collectively [150, 151]. In the asymptotic limit we would expect that decrease to manifest, with some eventual reduction in incompatibility. This is reinforced by the true incompatibility appearing to be at the lower end, with the NH bound being tight for n=1n=1 following from App. C, and appearing attainable numerically by the methods of Sec. 3.4 with |ℐNH−ℐSSW|≤3×10−3\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{NH}}-\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{SSW}}\rvert\leq 3{\times}10^{-3} for n≤4n\leq 4 [149].

Finally, we note that this growth in incompatibility, which may not represent the asymptotic behaviour, does come as the overall estimation precision increases, i.e., ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}} and its upper and lower bounds themselves decrease in the number of copies; see the plot of ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}} versus number of copies in the inset.

4.3 Qubit planar tomography

We conclude by analysing a configuration that, unlike the previous two examples, displays an a priori MSL larger than twice the SPM bound—the quantity leading to the upper bound on measurement incompatibility in Eq. (36). Before proceeding, we note that the purpose of this application is to illustrate specific mathematical properties of the theoretical bounds introduced, rather than to address a problem of physical relevance. For simplicity, we shall therefore use the MSL as a loss quantifier, notwithstanding the symmetry arguments discussed in Secs. 2.2 and 4.2.

Consider the following family of single-qubit states:

ρ⁡(𝜽)=12​(𝕀2+θ1​σx+θ2​σy),\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb{I}_{2}+\theta_{1}\sigma_{x}+\theta_{2}\sigma_{y}\right), (88)

where the unknown parameters satisfy the constraint θ12+θ22≤1\theta_{1}^{2}+\theta_{2}^{2}\leq 1 to ensure physicality. This setting corresponds to states lying on the plane z=0z=0 of the Bloch sphere, hence the term planar tomography. We assume independent, but not identical, prior distributions for the two parameters, i.e., p⁡(𝜽)=p1​(θ1)​p2​(θ2)p(\boldsymbol{\theta})=p_{1}(\theta_{1})\,p_{2}(\theta_{2}), where p1​(θ1)p_{1}(\theta_{1}) and p2​(θ2)p_{2}(\theta_{2}) are supported on [−W1,W1][-W_{1},W_{1}] and [−W2,W2][-W_{2},W_{2}], respectively. Overall, we have a bivariate distribution over a rectangle contained inside the Bloch circle in the x−yx-y plane, ensured by the condition W12+W22≤1W_{1}^{2}+W_{2}^{2}\leq 1. Finally, we assume that the prior for each parameter has zero mean and a finite second moment:

∫d​θi​pi​(θi)​θi=0,vi≔∫d​θi​pi​(θi)​θi2≤∞.\int\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{i}\,p_{i}(\theta_{i})\,\theta_{i}=0,\quad v_{i}\coloneq\int\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{i}\,p_{i}(\theta_{i})\,\theta_{i}^{2}\leq\infty. (89)

Under these assumptions, and choosing L=𝕀2L=\mathbb{I}_{2}, the a priori MSL is

ℒprior=λ=v1+v2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}=\lambda=v_{1}+v_{2}\,, (90)

while the zeroth and first state moments are

ρ0=𝕀2,ρ¯i=vi2​σi,\rho_{0}=\frac{\mathbb{I}}{2},\quad\bar{\rho}_{i}=\frac{v_{i}}{2}\sigma_{i}, (91)

where for simplicity we label Pauli matrices as σ1≡σx\sigma_{1}\equiv\sigma_{x} and σ2≡σy\sigma_{2}\equiv\sigma_{y}. Given that ρ0\rho_{0} is proportional to the identity, the SPM operators are trivially obtained:

Si=2​ρi¯=vi​σi.S_{i}=2\bar{\rho_{i}}=v_{i}\sigma_{i}. (92)

Since they do not commute; this estimation problem is impacted by measurement incompatibility. However, the Bayesian weak commutativity condition proposed in Eq. (75) does again hold.

The SPM lower bound on the MSL can next be calculated as

ℒSPM=λ−∑iTr⁡[ρ0​Si2]=λ−12​∑ivi2​Tr⁡[σi2]=v1+v2−(v12+v22).\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}&=\lambda-\sum_{i}\Tr\!\left[\rho_{0}S_{i}^{2}\right]\\ &=\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}v_{i}^{2}\Tr\!\left[\sigma_{i}^{2}\right]\\ &=v_{1}+v_{2}-\left(v_{1}^{2}+v_{2}^{2}\right).\end{split} (93)

The NH bound will be calculated numerically, as before.

Moving now to the upper bounds, in this scenario we have ℒPGM=2​ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}}=2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}, since ρ0\rho_{0} commutes with the first state moments, and the symmetric and square-root inner products are therefore identical. Unlike in the two previous applications, here we find that the upper bound 2​ℒSPM2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}} is not trivial when

ℒprior>2​ℒSPM⇔2​(v12+v22)>v1+v2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}>2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}\iff 2\left(v_{1}^{2}+v_{2}^{2}\right)>v_{1}+v_{2}. (94)

Nevertheless, in order to have a tighter upper bound, we also calculate the PGM with the optimal estimator in Eq. (39). Since here such a bound depends on the following quantity:

Tr⁡[ρ⁡(𝜽)​ρ0−12​ρ¯i​ρ0−12]2=(vi2​θi​Tr⁡[σi2])2=vi2​θi2,\Tr\left[\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bar{\rho}_{i}\rho_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right]^{2}=\left(\frac{v_{i}}{2}\,\theta_{i}\,\Tr[\sigma_{i}^{2}]\right)^{2}\\ =v_{i}^{2}\theta_{i}^{2}, (95)

the integrals over θi\theta_{i} with respect to the prior in Eq. (39) yield a further multiplication by the second moments viv_{i}, giving the final expression

ℒPGM∗=v1+v2−(v13+v23).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}^{*}}=v_{1}+v_{2}-\left(v_{1}^{3}+v_{2}^{3}\right). (96)

We now show a particular choice that satisfies the inequality (94). Let each independent prior be based on a symmetric beta distribution rescaled and translated such that it is supported on the interval [−Wi,Wi][-W_{i},W_{i}], and having zero mean as required:

pi​(θi)=12​Wi​hβ​(θi2​Wi+12),p_{i}(\theta_{i})=\frac{1}{2W_{i}}h_{\beta}\left(\frac{\theta_{i}}{2W_{i}}+\frac{1}{2}\right), (97)

where

hβ​(z)=(1−z)β−1​zβ−1B⁡(β,β),h_{\beta}(z)=\frac{(1-z)^{\beta-1}z^{\beta-1}}{B(\beta,\beta)}, (98)

β>0\beta>0 controls the shape,

B⁡(z1,z2)=∫01d​t​tz1−1​(1−t)z2−1=Γ⁡(z1)​Γ​(z2)Γ⁡(z1+z2)\begin{split}B(z_{1},z_{2})&=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}t\,t^{z_{1}-1}(1-t)^{z_{2}-1}\\ &=\frac{\Gamma(z_{1})\,\Gamma(z_{2})}{\Gamma(z_{1}+z_{2})}\end{split} (99)

is the beta function, and Γ⁡(z)\Gamma(z) is the gamma function. For such an a priori assignment, the variances are

vi=Wi21+2​β.v_{i}=\frac{W_{i}^{2}}{1+2\beta}. (100)

Therefore, by appropriately adjusting the parameters {Wi}\{W_{i}\} and β\beta, one can find regions where the inequality (94) is satisfied.

The incompatibility bounds corresponding to the MSL upper and lower bounds discussed above are plotted in Fig. 3, for various choices of the prior parameters W1W_{1}, W2W_{2} and β\beta. The graphical conventions distinguishing curves follow those established in Sec. 4.1. The region of incompatibility values permitted by the bounds is shaded in Fig. 3, however, for this class of models the NH bound is exactly attainable (see App. C), in analogy with local QET [88].

From these plots we observe that, when β\beta is sufficiently small—roughly speaking, the prior distribution becomes more concentrated towards the edges—the upper bound ℐ≤ℐPGM=1\mathcal{I}\leq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{PGM}}=1 becomes nontrivial as ℐprior\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{prior}} can exceed the value of 11. In particular, in the bottom panel of Fig. 3 we show that for β=0.07\beta=0.07 and W1=0.83W_{1}=0.83 the inequality ℐ≤1\mathcal{I}\leq 1 is not trivial for the whole range of valid values for the prior width 0<W2<1−W120<W_{2}<\sqrt{1-W_{1}^{2}}, such that W22+W12<1W_{2}^{2}+W_{1}^{2}<1.

5 Discussion

One important aspect that we have not addressed is the relationship between Bayesian QET and the bounds derived in local QET for the frequentist loss in Eq. (8). In this regard, we recall a conjecture of Ref. [10]: under appropriate regularity conditions, the Bayesian MSL and the frequentist loss would become asymptotically equivalent, that is,

limn→∞n​ℒmin(n)=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ℒH​(𝜽),\lim_{n\to\infty}n\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}^{(n)}=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), (101)

where ℒmin(n)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}^{(n)} is the MSL associated with nn copies of a given state, ρ⊗n​(𝜽)\rho^{\otimes n}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), and prior p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}), while ℒH​(𝜽)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is the HCRB of local QET77 7 Bounds in local QET are most commonly denoted by the letter CC, which stands for CRB—for example, CH​(𝜽)C_{\mathrm{H}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) for the HCRB. However, for consistency with the rest of this work we retain the terminology “loss” and the symbol ℒ\mathcal{L}, since these quantities bound the frequentist loss ℒ⁡(𝜽)\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) defined in Eq. (8).. This expression would represent the minimum achievable frequentist loss in the asymptotic limit of large nn.

Since in local QET it holds that [78, 79]

2​ℒS​(𝜽)≥ℒH​(𝜽)≥ℒS​(𝜽),2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), (102)

where ℒS​(𝜽)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is the Helstrom (SLD) CRB, our inequality in Eq. (35) is consistent with this asymptotic conjecture. Notice that, by definition, the Bayesian MSL ℒmin(n)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}^{(n)} is obtained by minimising over POVMs acting collectively on nn copies, dubbed “correlated measurements” in Ref. [95].

Despite increasing efforts in the experimental implementation of few-copy collective measurements [156, 151, 157, 158, 159, 160, 153], scaling them to large nn remains challenging in practice. Following this observation, recent work in local QET has addressed the minimum multiparameter frequentist loss achievable with single-copy measurements and classical feedback, referred to as “uncorrelated measurements” in Ref. [95]. This quantity corresponds to a minimisation of the weighted trace of the inverse Fisher information matrix (FIM) over all single-copy POVMs,

ℒmin​(𝜽)≔minM⁡(𝜽)⁡Tr⁡[L​F​(𝜽)−1],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\coloneq\min_{M(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\Tr[LF(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{-1}], (103)

where F⁡(𝜽)F(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is the FIM obtained by applying a POVM to a single copy ρ⁡(𝜽)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}). This is often called the “most informative” [87] or “tight” [95] bound.

Unlike the HCRB, ℒmin​(𝜽)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) can be larger than 2​ℒS​(𝜽)2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) [93, 95]. This appears to be in contrast with the Bayesian setting, where the inequality 2​ℒSPM≥ℒmin2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}} holds at the single-copy level as well. The resolution of this apparent tension comes from noticing that the ℒmin​(𝜽)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is still attainable only asymptotically, but restricting each copy to be measured independently, albeit adaptively with classical feedback from previous outcomes. Therefore, we expect that imposing an analogous restriction in the Bayesian case should lead to a similar behaviour as the number of shots increases. More concretely, we conjecture that, under suitable regularity conditions

limn→∞n​ℒmin(n),uncorr=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ℒmin​(𝜽),\lim_{n\to\infty}n\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}^{(n),\mathrm{uncorr}}=\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,, (104)

where ℒmin(n),uncorr\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}^{(n),\mathrm{uncorr}} would be the MSL for the prior p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and family of states ρ⊗n​(𝜽)\rho^{\otimes n}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), but minimised over the uncorrelated measurement strategies defined above, instead of arbitrary collective (correlated) POVMs over all the copies.

We conclude by noting that hybrid figures of merit, incorporating methods from both local and global QET, have been introduced [21, 161]. However, these approaches are mostly heuristic, and understanding the connections outlined in this discussion could clarify their exact range of applicability.

6 Conclusions and outlook

QET was initiated in the 1960s and 1970s, but only in recent years have several lines of research converged, leading to a deeper understanding of multiparameter aspects [10, 67, 69]. Building on this progress, in this work we have laid the foundations for a theory of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. We have achieved this by reviewing, streamlining, and contextualising existing results, and by deriving a number of new ones, including: the explicit set of conditions (19) that the optimal POVM must satisfy under the MSL criterion; the upper bound 2​ℒSPM2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}} on the minimum MSL in the first inequality of Eq. (35), showing that such a minimum can be at most twice the value of the bound when neglecting measurement incompatibility; the tighter upper bound through the PGM, and a tight bound on both ℒPGM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PGM}} and ℒprior\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}} using its POVM with the optimal PM estimator; the introduction of general PM operators and their corresponding matrix lower bounds via the monotonicity of inner products, presented in App. D; and finally, the demonstration that measurement incompatibility in a single-shot Bayesian setup is substantially affected by prior information, as illustrated through examples in qubit and optical configurations.

This work opens several avenues for future research that we now highlight, both theoretical and experimental. For example, in multiparameter quantum metrology—the simultaneous estimation of several parameters encoded by a quantum channel—additional precision trade-offs may arise from the choice of probe state and control strategy [124, 162, 95, 126], a phenomenon referred to as probe incompatibility [125]. While this aspect has not, to the best of our knowledge, been examined in detail and in full generality within a Bayesian framework, numerical approaches for designing optimal multiparameter Bayesian estimation protocols [106, 107, 163] inherently account for probe incompatibility effects.

Still outstanding are conditions that lead to collapse in the hierarchy of lower or upper bounds. Perhaps the most likely candidate would be the Bayesian weak commutativity condition proposed in Eq. (75), whose local QET analogue implies equivalence of the Helstrom (SLD) and Holevo CRBs. Entirely consistent with the Bayesian weak-commutativity condition implying saturability of the NH bound, all our examples satisfy Eq. (75) and the NH bound appears attainable. Incidentally, the Bayesian Holevo bound also matches the SPM bound numerically in all examples88 8 Supplemental data [149] shows that the Bayesian Holevo bound matches the SPM bound with |ℐH|≤2×10−7\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{H}}\rvert\leq 2{\times}10^{-7} for 2≤d≤172\leq d\ \leq 17 for the example considered in Sec. 4.1, with |ℐH|≤2×10−5\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{H}}\rvert\leq 2{\times}10^{-5} for 1≤n≤61\leq n\leq 6 (the Bayesian Holevo bound calculation becomes highly computationally demanding for larger nn) for the example considered in Sec. 4.2, and with |ℐH|≤3×10−5\lvert\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{H}}\rvert\leq 3{\times}10^{-5} for all points shown in Fig. 3., and—though not saturable and generally less significant in the Bayesian framework—this may be expected to hold more generally when the Bayesian weak-commutativity condition is satisfied, given the similarity of the underlying algebra.

Another important problem is addressing incompatibility—measurement and other forms thereof—for parameters obeying symmetries other than translation invariance. The symmetry remapping in Eq. (80) provides a starting point to generalise the results of this study to any location-isomorphic estimation problem, concrete illustrations of which have been discussed both in Sec. 4.2 and in Ref. [37]. A rigorous formulation should include the possibility of correlated priors and loss functions coupling different parameters, as well as the application of information geometry [119]. Moreover, a further extension to symmetries beyond location-isomorphic metrology is necessary to encompass phase parameters [120, 164].

In addition, while our analysis has focused on finite-dimensional systems, continuous-variable (CV) platforms—particularly quantum optical ones [6, 2, 165, 166]—play a central role in sensing applications. It will therefore be important to rigorously extend the theoretical framework developed here to CV systems. Given the rapid progress in learning theory for CV states [167, 168, 169, 170], this direction appears especially promising. For example, the case of Gaussian states and priors [103] may allow for a tractable analysis while remaining relevant for practical implementations. In single-parameter Bayesian estimation, several specific results for Gaussian states are already known [171], and a general framework for multiparameter local QET with Gaussian states—capable of giving incompatibility with collective measurements—has recently been proposed [172].

At a practical level, identifying optimal strategies for even an individual shot in an adaptive, experimental protocol can be computationally difficult. Even methods reducible to convex problems [107] are currently far less performant than solving the corresponding NH bound, in turn more demanding than the SPM and PGM lower and upper bounds. The upper bound ℒmin≤2​ℒSPM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}\leq 2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}} suggests that optimising the SPM affords a good compromise between optimality and tractability, compared to the exact but difficult minimum loss (20), with a smaller SPM bound also meaning a smaller upper bound on ℒmin\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}} and so the worst-case impact of measurement-incompatibility is smaller in absolute terms. In practice this sees the pseudo-gain Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ0​Si​Sj]L^{ij}\Tr[\rho_{0}S_{i}S_{j}]—i.e., the second term in the SPM lower bound (21); see App. A—become the optimiser of experimental control parameters for individual shots, fulfilling the role of a global alternative to the weighted trace of the inverse quantum FIM. Although such an approach will not generally lead to full optimality, we anticipate a substantial boost in quantum technological applications, in light of recent results from cold-atom experiments showing two-fold [36] and five-fold [37] precision enhancements obtained by employing the “classical” version of this quantifier, that is, the pseudo-gain computed using the PM estimator and a fixed POVM.

Altogether, we expect the Bayesian multiparameter framework for QET introduced here, together with the insight into the impact of measurement incompatibility, to become a fundamental building block for benchmarking both theory and experiment in quantum metrology, guiding the design of practically relevant, information-optimal quantum sensors.

Note added. During the preparation of the final version of this manuscript for publication, we became aware of the independent preprint by Zhang, Yamagata, and Suzuki [173], which develops a systematic theory of Bayesian monotone metrics and contains, among other results, a derivation of the monotone-metric matrix and scalar lower bounds presented in App. D. Revisiting our derivation, we found that an earlier version of App. D should have used complex, rather than only real, linear combinations of the parameter moments in order to justify the complex matrix inequality. We have amended the proof accordingly; the stated bounds are unchanged. Previous versions also specified an unnecessary property that linear maps EρE_{\rho} must satisfy; we thank Jun Suzuki for highlighting this. This property was not relied on in the subsequent proof.

Appendix A Prior loss and precision gain in Bayesian quantum estimation

Suppose we make a random guess of the unknown parameters based solely on the prior probability. Let us denote the corresponding vector of estimates by 𝜽~\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}, noting the absence of any outcome dependence. The MSL in this case is given by

ℒp​(𝜽~)≔∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​(𝜽~−𝜽)T​L​(𝜽~−𝜽),\mathcal{L}_{p}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\coloneq\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta})^{T}L\,(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}), (105)

which we may refer to as the prior loss. Alternatively, one may obtain Eq. (105) by inserting a trivial POVM consisting of a single element, the identity operator, into the MSL in Eq. (14).

It is straightforward to verify that the estimator minimising Eq. (105) is the prior mean,

𝝁≔∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝜽,\boldsymbol{\mu}\coloneq\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\theta}, (106)

which leads to the minimum prior loss

ℒprior≔\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}\coloneq ℒp​(𝝁)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{p}(\boldsymbol{\mu}) (107)
=\displaystyle= ∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝜽⊤​L​𝜽−𝝁T​L​𝝁\displaystyle\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}L\,\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{T}\,L\,\boldsymbol{\mu}
=\displaystyle= λ−𝝁T​L​𝝁,\displaystyle\lambda-\boldsymbol{\mu}^{T}\,L\,\boldsymbol{\mu},

where λ\lambda was already defined in Eq. (15). Such an optimal prior loss is nothing but tr⁡L​Σp\tr L\Sigma_{p}, where Σp\Sigma_{p} is the covariance matrix of the multivariate prior probability p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and we have introduced a lowercase trace of d×dd{\times}d matrices, tr\tr, distinct from the uppercase trace of operators acting on the physical Hilbert space of the system.

One may further show that μi=Tr⁡[ρ0​Si]\mu_{i}=\Tr[\rho_{0}S_{i}], where ρ0\rho_{0} and SiS_{i} are defined in Sec. 2.3. This, together with Eq. (106), allows us to rewrite the SPM bound in Eq. (21) as

ℒSPM=ℒprior−𝒢SPM,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPM}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prior}}-\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{SPM}}, (108)

where

𝒢SPM≔Li​j​(Tr⁡[ρ0​Sj​Si]−Tr⁡[ρ0​Sj]​Tr​[ρ0​Si]).\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{SPM}}\coloneq L^{ij}(\Tr[\rho_{0}S_{j}S_{i}]-\Tr[\rho_{0}S_{j}]\,\Tr[\rho_{0}S_{i}]). (109)

Written in this form, the SPM bound can be interpreted as the result of reducing the prior loss by the amount of precision gained through individually optimal measurements, 𝒢SPM\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{SPM}}.

Recent literature has referred to the quantity Li​j​Tr⁡[ρ0​Sj​Si]L^{ij}\Tr[\rho_{0}S_{j}S_{i}] as an alternative definition of precision gain when the SPM bound is used as an optimiser for control parameters [37, 122]. From a computational standpoint, this definition is often more convenient, and it has likewise been adopted in our code [113]. Accordingly, we refer to this quantity as the pseudo-gain, following the discussion above. Naturally, the gain and pseudo-gain coincide whenever the vector prior mean 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu} vanishes.

Appendix B Optimality conditions for the MSL

Let Mopt​(𝜽~)M_{\mathrm{opt}}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}) denote the optimal POVM for a Bayesian quantum multiparameter estimation problem. Following Holevo [26, 27, 127] and Helstrom [29, 9], a necessary and sufficient condition for such a POVM to exist is the existence of a Hermitian operator

Υ=∫d​𝜽~​Mopt​(𝜽~)​ϱ​(𝜽~)=∫d​𝜽~​ϱ​(𝜽~)​Mopt​(𝜽~),\Upsilon=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}\,M_{\mathrm{opt}}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\,\varrho(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}\,\varrho(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\,M_{\mathrm{opt}}(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}), (110)

with

ϱ⁡(𝜽~)≔∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ρ​(𝜽)​l​(𝜽~,𝜽),\varrho(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})\coloneq\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,l(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}},\boldsymbol{\theta}), (111)

that satisfies

ϱ⁡(𝜽~)−Υ⪰0\varrho(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})-\Upsilon\succeq 0 (112)

for all 𝜽~\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}. The minimum loss is then given by ℒmin=Tr⁡(Υ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{min}}=\Tr(\Upsilon). A discrete version of this optimality condition exists for hypothesis testing [97, 98], and a generalisation to convex functions has recently been proposed [99].

We now derive the explicit form of these conditions for the MSL. Using the notation introduced in Sec. 2.3, Eq. (111) becomes

ϱ⁡(𝜽~)=Λ+Li​j​(θ~j​θ~i​ρ0−2​θ~j​ρ¯i),\varrho(\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}})=\Lambda+L^{ij}\bigl(\tilde{\theta}_{j}\tilde{\theta}_{i}\rho_{0}-2\tilde{\theta}_{j}\bar{\rho}_{i}\bigr), (113)

where Tr⁡(Λ)=λ\Tr(\Lambda)=\lambda. Accordingly, the operator in Eq. (110) takes the form

Υ=Λ+Li​j​(Mopt,j​i​ρ0−2​Mopt,j​ρ¯i)=Λ+Li​j​(ρ0​Mopt,j​i−2​ρ¯j​Mopt,i).\Upsilon=\Lambda+L^{ij}\bigl(M_{\mathrm{opt},ji}\rho_{0}-2M_{\mathrm{opt},j}\bar{\rho}_{i}\bigr)=\Lambda+L^{ij}\bigl(\rho_{0}M_{\mathrm{opt},ji}-2\bar{\rho}_{j}M_{\mathrm{opt},i}\bigr). (114)

By adding both expressions for Υ\Upsilon and dividing by two, we obtain

Υ=Λ+12​Li​j​(Mopt,j​i​ρ0+ρ0​Mopt,j​i)−Mopt,j​ρ¯i−ρ¯j​Mopt,i.\Upsilon=\Lambda+\tfrac{1}{2}L^{ij}(M_{\mathrm{opt},ji}\rho_{0}+\rho_{0}M_{\mathrm{opt},ji})-M_{\mathrm{opt},j}\bar{\rho}_{i}-\bar{\rho}_{j}M_{\mathrm{opt},i}. (115)

Finally, inserting Eqs. (113) and (115) into Eq. (112), we obtain the conditions that any POVM optimal under the MSL criterion must satisfy:

Li​j​[(θ~j​θ~i​𝕀−Mopt,j​i)​ρ0+ρ0​(θ~j​θ~i​𝕀−Mopt,j​i)−2​(θ~j​𝕀−Mopt,j)​ρ¯i−2​ρ¯j​(θ~i​𝕀−Mopt,i)]⪰0,L^{ij}[(\tilde{\theta}_{j}\tilde{\theta}_{i}\mathbb{I}-M_{\mathrm{opt},ji})\rho_{0}+\rho_{0}(\tilde{\theta}_{j}\tilde{\theta}_{i}\mathbb{I}-M_{\mathrm{opt},ji})-2(\tilde{\theta}_{j}\mathbb{I}-M_{\mathrm{opt},j})\bar{\rho}_{i}-2\bar{\rho}_{j}(\tilde{\theta}_{i}\mathbb{I}-M_{\mathrm{opt},i})]\succeq 0, (116)

for all 𝜽~\boldsymbol{\tilde{\theta}}, as stated in the main text.

Appendix C Tightness of the NH bound for two parameters on a single qubit

In the main text we have shown that the Bayesian NH bound is obtained by relaxing the requirement that the first- and second-moment operators {Mi}\{M_{i}\} and {Mi​j}\{M_{ij}\} originate from an underlying POVM M⁡(x)M(x), exploiting the operator-valued moment-matrix inequality (42). In general, this relaxation can be loose. However, in this appendix we show that, for two parameters on a single qubit, the relaxation is instead exact, and it coincides with an attainability result proved by Nagaoka for 2×22{\times}2 matrices. Thus, this appendix shows that the reason for the tightness of Nagaoka’s two-parameter bound in local estimation naturally carries over to the Bayesian domain.

For d=2d=2 and the identity weight matrix L=𝕀2L=\mathbb{I}_{2} (without loss of generality; see footnote 4 in the main text), the optimisation over the second-moment operators M11,M12,M22M_{11},M_{12},M_{22} can be carried out analytically, leading to Eq. (45), which we reproduce here for convenience:

ℒNH=λ+minM1,M2⁡{Tr⁡[ρ0​(M12+M22)]+‖ρ0​[M1,M2]​ρ0‖1−2​Tr⁡[ρ¯1​M1+ρ¯2​M2]}.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}=\lambda+\min_{M_{1},M_{2}}\left\{\Tr\!\big[\rho_{0}(M_{1}^{2}+M_{2}^{2})\big]+\big\|\sqrt{\rho_{0}}[M_{1},M_{2}]\sqrt{\rho_{0}}\big\|_{1}-2\Tr\!\big[\bar{\rho}_{1}M_{1}+\bar{\rho}_{2}M_{2}\big]\right\}. (117)

Here, M1,M2M_{1},M_{2} are the operator-valued first moments, defined in Eq. (17) in the main text, and ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} is the trace norm. The only source of looseness is that, in the derivation of ℒNH\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NH}}, the pair (M1,M2)(M_{1},M_{2}) is treated as a free pair of Hermitian operators, constrained only indirectly through Eq. (42), without explicitly enforcing that it comes from a common POVM M⁡(x)M(x).

Nagaoka proved the following result, for which we adapt the notation to the one used in this paper:

Theorem (Ref. [88, Theorem 2]).

Fix a pair of Hermitian operators M1,M2M_{1},M_{2} acting on a two-dimensional Hilbert space, and consider the set of all POVMs M⁡(x1,x2)M(x_{1},x_{2}) on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} whose first moments match this pair:

∫dx1dx2M(x1,x2)xi=Mi,i=1,2.\int\!\mathrm{d}x_{1}\mathrm{d}x_{2}\,M(x_{1},x_{2})\,x_{i}=M_{i},\qquad i=1,2. (118)

Among these POVMs, define the minimal achievable “quadratic” second-moment cost ∑iTr⁡[ρ0​Mi​i]\sum_{i}\Tr[\rho_{0}M_{ii}] to be

C⋆​(M1,M2):=infM⁡(x1,x2)​s.t. (118)Tr⁡[ρ0​∫d​x1​d​x2​(x12+x22)​M​(x1,x2)].C^{\star}(M_{1},M_{2}):=\inf_{M(x_{1},x_{2})\ \text{s.t.\ \eqref{eq:app_A2}}}\Tr\!\left[\rho_{0}\int\!\mathrm{d}x_{1}\mathrm{d}x_{2}\,(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2})\,M(x_{1},x_{2})\right]. (119)

Then, for a qubit system, this infimum is attainable and admits the closed form

C⋆​(M1,M2)=Tr⁡[ρ0​(M12+M22)]+‖ρ0​[M1,M2]​ρ0‖1.C^{\star}(M_{1},M_{2})=\Tr\!\big[\rho_{0}(M_{1}^{2}+M_{2}^{2})\big]+\big\|\sqrt{\rho_{0}}[M_{1},M_{2}]\sqrt{\rho_{0}}\big\|_{1}\,. (120)

This means that, for any M1M_{1}, M2M_{2}, an MSL

ℒ=λ+Tr⁡[ρ0​(M12+M22)]+‖ρ0​[M1,M2]​ρ0‖1−2​Tr⁡[ρ¯1​M1+ρ¯2​M2]\mathcal{L}=\lambda+\Tr\!\big[\rho_{0}(M_{1}^{2}+M_{2}^{2})\big]+\big\|\sqrt{\rho_{0}}[M_{1},M_{2}]\sqrt{\rho_{0}}\big\|_{1}-2\Tr\!\big[\bar{\rho}_{1}M_{1}+\bar{\rho}_{2}M_{2}\big] (121)

is attainable, which entails attainability of the Bayesian NH lower bound Eq. (117). Nagaoka also provided explicitly an optimal POVM attaining the equality above. Notice that this result is proven under the assumption ρ0≻0\rho_{0}\succ 0, which, for qubit systems, holds in essentially all nontrivial cases. The only exception arises when the prior is a Dirac delta, in which case the estimation problem becomes trivial.

The Bayesian NH bound is obtained by optimising over {Mi}\{M_{i}\} and {Mi​j}\{M_{ij}\} subject to the moment-matrix inequality (42), instead of optimising over POVMs directly. For two parameters, Eq. (45) (restated as Eq. (117)) already encodes the best possible contribution of second moments compatible with a given pair (M1,M2)(M_{1},M_{2}), namely Eq. (120). Therefore, in the qubit case for every candidate pair (M1,M2)(M_{1},M_{2}), there exists a POVM whose second moments attain the value Tr⁡[ρ0​(M12+M22)]+‖ρ0​[M1,M2]​ρ0‖1\Tr[\rho_{0}(M_{1}^{2}+M_{2}^{2})]+\|\sqrt{\rho_{0}}[M_{1},M_{2}]\sqrt{\rho_{0}}\|_{1}; hence the minimisation in Eq. (117) is not merely a relaxation: it coincides with the true minimum MSL over single-qubit POVMs. Operationally, one may view Eq. (117) as first optimising over the “effective first-moment operators” M1,M2M_{1},M_{2}, and then invoking Nagaoka’s construction to realise the corresponding optimal second moments by a concrete measurement on the qubit.

C.1 Explicit optimal POVM attaining the two parameter single qubit NH bound

For completeness, we briefly give the details of an explicit POVM attaining Eq. (120) for any fixed Hermitian pair (M1,M2)(M_{1},M_{2}) on a qubit with a full-rank ρ0\rho_{0}. We assume that M1M_{1} and M2M_{2} are linearly independent and non-commuting; otherwise, the problem is trivial, as they would share a common eigenbasis and the SPM bound would therefore be tight. Let x:=Tr⁡[ρ0​M1]x:=\Tr[\rho_{0}M_{1}] and y:=Tr⁡[ρ0​M2]y:=\Tr[\rho_{0}M_{2}] in order to define the centred operators X:=M1−x​𝕀2X:=M_{1}-x\mathbb{I}_{2} and Y:=M2−y​𝕀2Y:=M_{2}-y\mathbb{I}_{2}, so that Tr⁡[ρ0​X]=Tr⁡[ρ0​Y]=0\Tr[\rho_{0}X]=\Tr[\rho_{0}Y]=0. Introduce an inner product induced by the state ρ0\rho_{0} (see the next section for more details on such inner products)

⟨A,B⟩ρ0S,(e):=12​Tr⁡[ρ0​(A​B+B​A)],\langle A,B\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{\mathrm{S},(e)}:=\frac{1}{2}\Tr\left[\rho_{0}\left(AB+BA\right)\right], (122)

and let 𝒲:=spanℝ​{X,Y}\mathcal{W}:=\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{X,Y\}, i.e., the two-dimensional subspace of Hermitian operators with zero first moments spanned by XX and YY. Define a linear map 𝖠:𝒲→𝒲\mathsf{A}:\mathcal{W}\to\mathcal{W} as

𝖠⁡(W):=⟨W,X⟩ρ0S,(e)​X+⟨W,Y⟩ρ0S,(e)​Y.\mathsf{A}(W):=\langle W,X\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{\mathrm{S},(e)}\,X\;+\;\langle W,Y\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{\mathrm{S},(e)}\,Y. (123)

This map is symmetric and positive definite with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ρ0S,(e)\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{\mathrm{S},(e)}, hence it has an orthonormal eigenbasis of Hermitian operators {U1,U2}⊂𝒲\{U_{1},U_{2}\}\subset\mathcal{W} with eigenvalues ν1,ν2>0\nu_{1},\nu_{2}>0 satisfying 𝖠⁡(Uj)=νj​Uj\mathsf{A}(U_{j})=\nu_{j}U_{j} and ⟨Uj,Uk⟩ρ0S,(e)=δj​k\langle U_{j},U_{k}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{\mathrm{S},(e)}=\delta_{jk}.

Now, the optimal POVM can be obtained as a random projective measurement on the eigenbasis of U1U_{1} and U2U_{2}. Explicitly, diagonalise each UjU_{j} as Uj=∑k=12uj​k​Ej​kU_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{2}u_{jk}E_{jk}, where uj​k∈ℝu_{jk}\in\mathbb{R} are eigenvalues and Ej​kE_{jk} are rank-one projectors with ∑k=12Ej​k=𝕀2\sum_{k=1}^{2}E_{jk}=\mathbb{I}_{2}. Define

pj:=νjν1+ν2,M⁡(j,k):=pj​Ej​k,p_{j}:=\frac{\sqrt{\nu_{j}}}{\sqrt{\nu_{1}}+\sqrt{\nu_{2}}},\qquad M(j,k):=p_{j}\,E_{jk}, (124)

so that {M⁡(j,k)}j,k∈{1,2}\{M(j,k)\}_{j,k\in\{1,2\}} is a 4-outcome POVM satisfying ∑j,kM⁡(j,k)=𝕀2\sum_{j,k}M(j,k)=\mathbb{I}_{2} . Now, introducing the coefficients

xj​k:=pj−1​⟨X,Uj⟩ρ0S,(e)​uj​k+x,yj​k:=pj−1​⟨Y,Uj⟩ρ0S,(e)​uj​k+y,x_{jk}:=p_{j}^{-1}\,\langle X,U_{j}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{\mathrm{S},(e)}\,u_{jk}+x,\qquad y_{jk}:=p_{j}^{-1}\,\langle Y,U_{j}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{\mathrm{S},(e)}\,u_{jk}+y, (125)

the first-moment constraints hold as follows: ∑j,kxj​k​M​(j,k)=M1\sum_{j,k}x_{jk}M(j,k)=M_{1} and ∑j,kyj​k​M​(j,k)=M2\sum_{j,k}y_{jk}M(j,k)=M_{2}. It can be checked that the second-moment cost for this POVM and coefficients {xj​k,yj​k}\{x_{jk},y_{jk}\} attains the minimum in Eq. (119):

Tr⁡[ρ0​∑j​k(xj​k2+yj​k2)​M​(j,k)]=x2+y2+(ν1+ν2)2=x2+y2+Tr⁡[ρ0​(X2+Y2)]+‖ρ0​[X,Y]​ρ0‖1;\Tr\left[\rho_{0}\sum_{jk}(x_{jk}^{2}+y_{jk}^{2})M(j,k)\right]=x^{2}+y^{2}+(\sqrt{\nu_{1}}+\sqrt{\nu_{2}})^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+\Tr[\rho_{0}(X^{2}+Y^{2})]+\left\|\sqrt{\rho_{0}}[X,Y]\sqrt{\rho_{0}}\right\|_{1}; (126)

this matches Eq. (120), since x2+y2+Tr⁡[ρ0​(X2+Y2)]=Tr⁡[ρ0​(M12+M22)]x^{2}+y^{2}+\Tr[\rho_{0}(X^{2}+Y^{2})]=\Tr[\rho_{0}(M_{1}^{2}+M_{2}^{2})], and [X,Y]=[M1,M2][X,Y]=[M_{1},M_{2}].

C.2 Closed form of the qubit NH bound

We now show that, for two parameters and a single qubit, the remaining minimisation in Eq. (117) also admits a closed form. We only prove the result for L=𝕀2L=\mathbb{I}_{2}, as the bounds for other loss matrices can be obtained simply by reparametrization of the first moment operators (see footnote 4 in the main text).

Let SiS_{i} be the SPM operators for the qubit model, i.e., ρ¯i=Eρ0,S​[Si]=Si​ρ0+ρ0​Si2\bar{\rho}_{i}=E_{\rho_{0},\mathrm{S}}[S_{i}]=\frac{S_{i}\rho_{0}+\rho_{0}S_{i}}{2} with i=1,2i=1,2, and also introduce their zero-mean version Δ​Si:=Si−μi​𝕀2\Delta S_{i}:=S_{i}-\mu_{i}\mathbb{I}_{2}, where μi=Tr⁡[ρ0​Si]\mu_{i}=\Tr[\rho_{0}S_{i}] are the prior mean values in Eq. (106). Introducing the real 2×22\times 2 Gram matrix of the zero-mean SPM operators

Appendix D Matrix lower bounds from monotone metrics

D.1 Brief overview of monotone metrics

In this subsection we follow the notation of Ref. [112, Ch. 6.1], but see Ref. [137] for a recent survey on the topic of monotone metrics. For a given quantum state ρ\rho, we define an inner product as follows:

⟨Y,X⟩ρ(e)≔Tr⁡[Y†​Eρ​[X]],\langle Y,\,X\rangle_{\rho}^{(e)}\;\coloneq\;\Tr\left[Y^{\dagger}\,E_{\rho}[X]\right], (151)

where EρE_{\rho} is a linear map satisfying

Tr⁡[X†​Eρ​[X]]\displaystyle\Tr\left[X^{\dagger}E_{\rho}[X]\right] ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (152)
Tr⁡[Y†​Eρ​[X]]\displaystyle\Tr\left[Y^{\dagger}E_{\rho}[X]\right] =Tr⁡[Eρ​[Y]†​X],\displaystyle=\Tr\left[E_{\rho}[Y]^{\dagger}\,X\right], (153)

and

Eρ​[U†​X​U]\displaystyle E_{\rho}\left[U^{\dagger}XU\right] =U†​EU​ρ​U†​[X]​U,\displaystyle=U^{\dagger}\,E_{\,U\rho U^{\dagger}}\!\left[X\right]\,U, (154)
Eρ​[𝕀]\displaystyle E_{\rho}\left[\mathbb{I}\right] =ρ,\displaystyle=\rho, (155)

Following Hayashi’s formulation, these maps and inner products are defined on arbitrary finite-dimensional operators, so XX and YY need not be Hermitian. The choice of the map EρE_{\rho} determines the inner product. We will primarily work with a generic one; however, three notable examples are:

Eρ,S​[X]\displaystyle E_{\rho,\mathrm{S}}[X] =12​(X​ρ+ρ​X)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(X\rho+\rho X\right) (156)
Eρ,R​[X]\displaystyle E_{\rho,\mathrm{R}}[X] =X​ρ\displaystyle=X\rho (157)
Eρ,sq​[X]\displaystyle E_{\rho,\mathrm{sq}}[X] =ρ​X​ρ,\displaystyle=\sqrt{\rho}X\sqrt{\rho}, (158)

which we will call “symmetric”, “right” and “square-root”, respectively. As in the main text, we assume ρ≻0\rho\succ 0 and for the standard monotone maps we will consider next it ensures that EρE_{\rho} is invertible, so that we can introduce the dual inner product in terms of the inverse linear map Eρ−1E_{\rho}^{-1} without further regularisations:

⟨A,B⟩ρ(m)=Tr⁡[Eρ−1​[A]†​B];\langle A,\,B\rangle_{\rho}^{(m)}\;=\;\Tr\left[E_{\rho}^{-1}[A]^{\dagger}B\right]; (159)

it is denoted by the superscript (m)(m), following Hayashi’s notation. More specifically, in what follows we consider inner products with the standard classical normalisation: when ρ\rho and X,YX,Y are diagonal in the same basis, the dual inner product reduces to the classical Fisher-type expression ⟨X,Y⟩ρ(m)=∑kXk​k∗​Yk​kρk​k\langle X,Y\rangle_{\rho}^{(m)}=\sum_{k}\frac{X_{kk}^{*}Y_{kk}}{\rho_{kk}}.

One of the crucial properties of such dual inner products is the monotonicity under the action of quantum channels, which makes them a good measure of information. In the following, we restrict to choices of EρE_{\rho} belonging to the standard class of monotone quantum metrics characterised by Petz [136, 137], or more generally to maps whose dual inner products satisfy the data-processing inequality99 9 Petz’s work gives a complete characterisation of normalised monotone Riemannian metrics on the tangent space of full-rank quantum states, i.e., on Hermitian traceless operators. Here we also use the associated inner products on the full operator space, so we explicitly assume that the chosen extension continues to satisfy Eq. (160).:

⟨A,A⟩ρ(m)≥⟨Λ⁡[A],Λ⁡[A]⟩Λ⁡[ρ](m),\langle A,A\rangle_{\rho}^{(m)}\geq\langle\Lambda[A],\Lambda[A]\rangle_{\Lambda[\rho]}^{(m)}\,, (160)

where Λ\Lambda is a quantum channel, i.e., a completely positive trace-preserving map, such that also the output state is full rank Λ⁡[ρ]≻0\Lambda[\rho]\succ 0. In the derivation below we will only use classical normalisation and this data-processing inequality.

For normalised monotone metrics in the Petz class, another important property which holds for Hermitian operators A=A†A=A^{\dagger} is that the norm induced by this class of inner products is minimal and maximal for the symmetric and right versions, respectively:

⟨A,A⟩ρS,(m)≤⟨A,A⟩ρ(m)≤⟨A,A⟩ρR,(m).\langle A,A\rangle_{\rho}^{\mathrm{S},(m)}\,\leq\langle A,A\rangle^{(m)}_{\rho}\,\leq\langle A,A\rangle_{\rho}^{\mathrm{R},(m)}\,. (161)

Eq. (33) in the main text follows from the first inequality. In the derivation of the matrix lower bounds below, where complex linear combinations of posterior moments are used, we only rely on the monotonicity property (160), which holds for arbitrary operators.

D.2 Posterior mean operators

Introducing the MSL matrix, with elements

Σi​j=∫d​x​∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽,x)​(θ~i​(x)−θi)​(θ~j​(x)−θj),\Sigma_{ij}=\int\!\mathrm{d}x\,\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta},x)\,(\tilde{\theta}_{i}(x)-\theta_{i})(\tilde{\theta}_{j}(x)-\theta_{j})\,, (162)

where p⁡(𝜽,x)=p⁡(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta},x)=p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta}), the scalar MSL can be written as

ℒ=Li​j​Σj​i=tr⁡L​Σ.\mathcal{L}=L^{ij}\Sigma_{ji}=\tr L\Sigma\,. (163)

Classically, and thus also for quantum problems where the measurement is fixed, the optimal Bayes estimator that minimises the multiparameter MSL matrix is the PM:

θ~opt,i​(x)=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽|x)​θi=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽)​θi∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽),\tilde{\theta}_{\mathrm{opt},i}(x)=\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta}|x)\,\theta_{i}=\frac{\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{i}}{\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})}, (164)

which was already defined in Eq. (26) of the main text. Applying this estimator, the optimal MSL matrix has elements

Σi​j=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​θi​θj−∫d​x​[∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽)​θi]​[∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽)​θj]∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽).\Sigma_{ij}=\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{i}\theta_{j}-\int\!\mathrm{d}x\,\frac{\left[\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{i}\right]\left[\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{j}\right]}{\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})}\,. (165)

Following Ref. [43], we now proceed to consider the positive scalar

𝒖†​Σ​𝒖=u∗i​uj​Σi​j=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​|θ𝒖|2−∫d​x​|∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽)​θ𝒖|2∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​p​(x|𝜽),\boldsymbol{u}^{\dagger}\Sigma\boldsymbol{u}=u^{*i}u^{j}\Sigma_{ij}=\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,|\theta_{\boldsymbol{u}}|^{2}-\int\!\mathrm{d}x\,\frac{\left|\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{\boldsymbol{u}}\right|^{2}}{\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})}, (166)

where 𝒖∈ℂd\boldsymbol{u}\in\mathbb{C}^{d} is a complex vector and θ𝒖=𝒖†​𝜽=u∗i​θi\theta_{\boldsymbol{u}}=\boldsymbol{u}^{\dagger}\boldsymbol{\theta}=u^{*i}\theta_{i} is a linear combination of parameters. For quantum systems, the outcome probability for a given value of the parameters is obtained from Born’s rule p⁡(x|𝜽)=Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ​(𝜽)]p(x|\boldsymbol{\theta})=\Tr\left[M(x)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right], which leads to a complexified version of Eq. (6) in Ref. [43]:

𝒖†​Σ​𝒖=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​|θ𝒖|2−∫d​x​|Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ¯𝒖]|2Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ0],\boldsymbol{u}^{\dagger}\Sigma\boldsymbol{u}=\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,|\theta_{\boldsymbol{u}}|^{2}-\int\!\mathrm{d}x\,\frac{\left|\Tr\left[M(x)\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}\right]\right|^{2}}{\Tr\left[M(x)\rho_{0}\right]}\,, (167)

where ρ¯𝒖=u∗i​ρ¯i=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​ρ​(𝜽)​θ𝒖\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}=u^{*i}\bar{\rho}_{i}=\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\theta_{\boldsymbol{u}}.

The same result can be arrived at from the formalism of Sec. 2.3 with the posterior mean estimator Eq. (11) being

θ~j​(x)=Tr⁡[ρ¯j​M​(x)]Tr⁡[ρ0​M​(x)],\tilde{\theta}_{j}(x)=\frac{\Tr[\bar{\rho}_{j}M(x)]}{\Tr[\rho_{0}M(x)]},

assuming a parameter-independent measurement. As such, the operators MjM_{j} and Mj​kM_{jk} introduced in Eq. (17) take the form

Mi\displaystyle M_{i} =∫d​x​M​(x)​Tr⁡[ρ¯i​M​(x)]Tr⁡[ρ0​M​(x)],\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}x\,M(x)\,\frac{\Tr[\bar{\rho}_{i}M(x)]}{\Tr[\rho_{0}M(x)]}, Mi​j\displaystyle M_{ij} =∫d​x​M​(x)​Tr⁡[ρ¯i​M​(x)]​Tr⁡[ρ¯j​M​(x)]Tr⁡[ρ0​M​(x)]2;\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}x\,M(x)\,\frac{\Tr[\bar{\rho}_{i}M(x)]\Tr[\bar{\rho}_{j}M(x)]}{\Tr[\rho_{0}M(x)]^{2}}; (168)

the application in Eq. (14) then leads to Eq. (167).

A crucial observation from Ref. [43] is that the second term resembles the classical Fisher information and so it is possible to apply a Braunstein–Caves–like inequality [71] and obtain a matrix SPM lower bound on Σ\Sigma. Here, we take a different route and use a more general family of inequalities which stem from the monotonicity of the inner products defined in the previous sections. This allows us to derive a whole family of matrix lower bounds, similarly to the case of local QET.

For simplicity, we focus on a discrete set of measurement outcomes xx, which can always be encoded on a register composed by an orthonormal basis of vectors {|ex⟩}\{\ket{e_{x}}\}. We introduce the measurement channel

κ[∙]≔∑xTr[M(x)∙]|ex⟩⟨ex|;\kappa[\bullet]\coloneq\sum_{x}\Tr[M(x)\bullet]|e_{x}\rangle\langle e_{x}|\,; (169)

this is an entanglement-breaking quantum channel that formally represents the map between quantum states and probability distributions (diagonal quantum states) implemented by the POVM with elements M⁡(x)M(x). Outcomes with Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ0]=0\Tr[M(x)\rho_{0}]=0 can be discarded, or equivalently one works on the support of κ⁡[ρ0]\kappa[\rho_{0}]. Applying this channel to ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ¯𝒖\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}} we obtain

κ⁡[ρ0]=∑xTr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ0]​|ex⟩​⟨ex|,κ⁡[ρ¯𝒖]=∑xTr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ¯𝒖]​|ex⟩​⟨ex|.\begin{split}\kappa[\rho_{0}]&=\sum_{x}\Tr\left[M(x)\rho_{0}\right]|e_{x}\rangle\langle e_{x}|,\\ \kappa[\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}]&=\sum_{x}\Tr\left[M(x)\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}\right]|e_{x}\rangle\langle e_{x}|.\end{split} (170)

These operators are diagonal in the orthonormal basis {|ex⟩}\{\ket{e_{x}}\} and they commute with each other; hence, by the classical normalisation stated above, the dual inner product gives exactly the second term of Eq. (167):

⟨κ⁡[ρ¯𝒖],κ⁡[ρ¯𝒖]⟩κ⁡[ρ0](m)=Tr⁡[Eκ⁡[ρ0]−1​(κ⁡[ρ¯𝒖])†​κ​[ρ¯𝒖]]=∑x|Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ¯𝒖]|2Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ0].\langle\kappa[\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}],\kappa[\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}]\rangle^{(m)}_{\kappa[\rho_{0}]}=\Tr\left[E_{\kappa[\rho_{0}]}^{-1}(\kappa[\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}])^{\dagger}\kappa[\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}]\right]=\sum_{x}\frac{\left|\Tr\left[M(x)\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}\right]\right|^{2}}{\Tr\left[M(x)\rho_{0}\right]}. (171)

Therefore, by the monotonicity property (160) we finally obtain that

∑x|Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ¯𝒖]|2Tr⁡[M⁡(x)​ρ0]≤⟨ρ¯𝒖,ρ¯𝒖⟩ρ0(m)=⟨L𝒖,L𝒖⟩ρ0(e),\sum_{x}\frac{\left|\Tr\left[M(x)\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}\right]\right|^{2}}{\Tr\left[M(x)\rho_{0}\right]}\leq\langle\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}},\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}\rangle^{(m)}_{\rho_{0}}=\langle L_{\boldsymbol{u}},L_{\boldsymbol{u}}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{(e)}, (172)

where now L𝒖L_{\boldsymbol{u}} is a generic PM operator obtained as

L𝒖≔Eρ0−1​[ρ¯𝒖]=u∗i​Eρ0−1​[ρ¯i]=u∗i​Li,L_{\boldsymbol{u}}\coloneq E^{-1}_{\rho_{0}}[\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}]=u^{*i}E^{-1}_{\rho_{0}}[\bar{\rho}_{i}]=u^{*i}L_{i}, (173)

where we have also introduced PM operators for each original parameter, satisfying the equations Eρ0​(Li)=ρ¯iE_{\rho_{0}}(L_{i})=\bar{\rho}_{i}. Such PM operators generalise the symmetric version introduced in the main text in terms of the map Eρ,SE_{\rho,\mathrm{S}}. For example, they also include the operators introduced in Ref. [105, Theorem 8], where they are called “λ\lambda logarithmic derivatives”.

From the inequality in Eq. (172), the lower bound for the scalar introduced before immediately follows:

𝒖†​Σ​𝒖≥∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​|θ𝒖|2−𝒖†​𝒦​𝒖,\boldsymbol{u}^{\dagger}\Sigma\boldsymbol{u}\geq\int\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\left|\theta_{\boldsymbol{u}}\right|^{2}-\boldsymbol{u}^{\dagger}\mathcal{K}\boldsymbol{u}, (174)

where we have introduced the complex-valued Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix with elements

𝒦i​j≔⟨ρ¯j,ρ¯i⟩ρ0(m)=⟨Lj,Li⟩ρ0(e)=Tr⁡[Lj†​Eρ0​[Li]];\mathcal{K}_{ij}\coloneq\langle\bar{\rho}_{j},\bar{\rho}_{i}\rangle^{(m)}_{\rho_{0}}=\langle L_{j},L_{i}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{(e)}=\Tr[L_{j}^{\dagger}E_{\rho_{0}}[L_{i}]]\,; (175)

notice that with this index convention, 𝒖†​𝒦​𝒖=⟨ρ¯𝒖,ρ¯𝒖⟩ρ0(m)≥0\boldsymbol{u}^{\dagger}\mathcal{K}\boldsymbol{u}=\langle\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}},\bar{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{u}}\rangle_{\rho_{0}}^{(m)}\geq 0. By choosing the map Eρ,SE_{\rho,\mathrm{S}}, this matrix becomes the real-valued SPM matrix introduced in Ref. [43]. However, for other choices, such as Eρ,RE_{\rho,\mathrm{R}}, this matrix is still Hermitian but complex-valued. Regardless of the particular choice of monotone metric, since the scalar inequality holds for an arbitrary choice of 𝒖∈ℂd\boldsymbol{u}\in\mathbb{C}^{d}, we obtain the family of matrix lower bounds on the MSL matrix

Σ⪰∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝜽​𝜽T−𝒦.\Sigma\succeq\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\theta}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}-\mathcal{K}\;. (176)

This is again a generalisation of the SPM matrix bound obtained in Ref. [43].

D.3 Scalar bounds from matrix inequalities

We start from the matrix inequality in Eq. (176) and denote the right-hand side by the symbol ℬ≔∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝜽​𝜽⊤−𝒦\mathcal{B}\coloneq\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\theta}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}-\mathcal{K}, where 𝒦≥0\mathcal{K}\geq 0 is a complex-valued Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix. We now want to show that also the imaginary part of 𝒦\mathcal{K} sets constraints on the minimum MSL ℒ\mathcal{L}. This fact is well-known [120]; for completeness, we provide a proof here, roughly following Ref. [10].

First, let us rewrite the function to minimise, subject to the constraint (176), as the trace of a symmetric matrix tr⁡L​Σ=tr⁡L​Σ​L\tr L\Sigma=\tr\sqrt{L}\Sigma\sqrt{L}. From (176) we can obtain the two matrix inequalities

L​Σ​L≥L​(Re⁡ℬ±i​Im⁡ℬ)​L,\sqrt{L}\,\Sigma\sqrt{L}\geq\sqrt{L}\left(\Re{\mathcal{B}}\pm i\Im{\mathcal{B}}\right)\sqrt{L}, (177)

where the two signs correspond to taking the transpose of the two sides of the original equation. Here Re⁡ℬ\Re\mathcal{B} and Im⁡ℬ\Im\mathcal{B} denote the entrywise real and imaginary parts, so that Re⁡ℬ\Re\mathcal{B} is real symmetric and Im⁡ℬ\Im\mathcal{B} is real antisymmetric. Now, this matrix inequality implies

∑k𝒛k†L(Σ−Reℬ)L𝒛k≥±∑k𝒛k†(iLImℬL)𝒛k,\sum_{k}\boldsymbol{z}_{k}^{\dagger}\sqrt{L}\left(\Sigma-\Re{\mathcal{B}}\right)\sqrt{L}\boldsymbol{z}_{k}\geq\pm\sum_{k}\boldsymbol{z}_{k}^{\dagger}\left(i\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{L}\right)\boldsymbol{z}_{k}\,, (178)

for any set of complex-valued vectors {𝒛i}\{\boldsymbol{z}_{i}\}. Since i​L​Im⁡ℬ​Li\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{L} is Hermitian, we can choose its eigenbasis as the vectors 𝒛i\boldsymbol{z}_{i}; noting the corresponding eigenvalues as λi\lambda_{i}, we obtain

tr⁡L⁡(Σ−Re⁡ℬ)≥∑i|λi|=tr|L​Im​ℬ​L|=‖L​Im​ℬ​L‖1.\displaystyle\tr L(\Sigma-\Re{\mathcal{B}})\geq\sum_{i}|\lambda_{i}|=\tr|\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{L}|=\|\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{L}\|_{1}. (179)

The absolute values are obtained by applying the positive inequality separately to eigenvectors with positive eigenvalues and the negative inequality separately to eigenvectors with negative eigenvalues, and then summing the resulting inequalities. The matrix |L​Im⁡ℬ​L||\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{L}|, where |A|≔A†​A|A|\coloneq\sqrt{A^{\dagger}A} denotes the operator absolute value, is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix that can be diagonalised in the same eigenbasis as i​L​Im⁡ℬ​Li\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{L}, with eigenvalues |λi||\lambda_{i}|. Moreover, ‖A‖1=tr⁡|A|=tr⁡A†​A\|A\|_{1}=\tr|A|=\tr\sqrt{A^{\dagger}A} is the Schatten 1-norm, also known as the trace norm or nuclear norm. This inequality for the trace of the real part of a positive semidefinite complex matrix is known as the Belavkin–Grishanin inequality [102, 78].

Assuming L≻0L\succ 0 (otherwise one should restrict to the support of LL), the minimum can be achieved by setting

Σ=Re⁡ℬ+L−1​|L​Im⁡ℬ​L|​L−1,\Sigma=\Re{\mathcal{B}}+\sqrt{L^{-1}}|\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{L}|\sqrt{L^{-1}}\,, (180)

as seen from direct computation.

In conclusion, we have proven that

minΣ≥ℬ⁡tr⁡L​Σ=tr⁡L​Re​ℬ+‖L​Im​ℬ​L‖1.\min_{\Sigma\geq\mathcal{B}}\tr L\Sigma=\tr L\Re{\mathcal{B}}+\|\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{B}}\sqrt{L}\|_{1}. (181)

Substituting back the original right-hand side of the inequality (176), we get

ℒ≥λ−Tr⁡[L​Re⁡𝒦]+‖L​Im⁡𝒦​L‖1,\mathcal{L}\geq\lambda-\Tr[L\Re{\mathcal{K}}]+\|\sqrt{L}\Im{\mathcal{K}}\sqrt{L}\|_{1}, (182)

since λ=tr⁡L​∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝜽​𝜽T=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝜽)​𝜽T​L​𝜽\lambda=\tr L\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\theta}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}=\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{T}L\,\boldsymbol{\theta}, and Im⁡ℬ=−Im⁡𝒦\Im{\mathcal{B}}=-\Im{\mathcal{K}}, given that the other matrix terms are real-valued by assumption. In general, this bound is not necessarily tight, as it is not always possible to find a measurement and estimator that produce a MSL matrix as in (180).

We finally note that the bound in Ref. [105, Theorem 8] in terms of the λ\lambda logarithmic derivatives is also in the class of scalar bounds derived in this Appendix.
